The new token is also not what the client uses: jsforce.Connection is still created with credentialKey.access_token (the pre-refresh value) at line 106, and a new refresh_token from Salesforce is discarded in favor of the old one. Every calendar operation also pays an extra token round-trip, and this path never calls refreshOAuthTokens, so CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is ignored for Salesforce.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Lark deletes the credential if the local refresh token is expired, before sync

refreshAccessToken still deletes the credential and throws when refresh_token is missing or refresh_expires_date is past, and only then calls refreshOAuthTokens. Credential sync is supposed to obtain a new access token from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without a provider refresh token (that helper's comment says the response only contains an access token and expiry). For a synced Lark user whose stored refresh token is a placeholder or has expired, the row is deleted and the sync endpoint is never called, so the integration and its tokens are lost instead of refreshed.

No tests cover token persistence or the credential webhook

The PR adds the credential webhook, parseRefreshTokenResponse, and refreshOAuthTokens, and the author notes that no tests were added. There is no unit test that the object written to credential.key is still the provider credential (Google currently persists the SafeParse wrapper) or that a refresh response without refresh_token keeps the previous refresh token (Office 365 now stores the literal "refresh_token"). Those regressions ship on the normal, sync-disabled refresh path and would be caught by a test that asserts the saved key.

Outbound token sync request carries no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug as form fields. It does not send CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, a signature, or any other credential, and it does not require HTTPS. .env.example presents this as configuration-only, and the helper comment says the response should contain the access token. Anyone who can reach that URL can request third-party access tokens for any Cal user id. Those tokens are then stored and used as the user's Google/Zoom/Microsoft credentials. The inbound webhook authenticates with a shared secret, but the outbound call that actually returns live tokens does not.

Sync update leaves invalid credentials marked invalid

When a credential already exists, the webhook updates only key. It does not set invalid: false. Adapters in this PR (Google, Webex, Zoom) set invalid: true after an unrecoverable refresh, and credential loading skips invalid rows. A later successful sync from the parent app therefore stores new tokens on a row that is still treated as disconnected, so calendar and video calls keep failing until the user deletes and reinstalls the app.

Webhook find-then-create can insert duplicate app credentials

The handler loads an existing credential with findFirst on (userId, appId) and, if none is found, creates one. There is no unique constraint on that pair (other OAuth callbacks in this PR delete duplicates because findFirst otherwise ignores them) and no transaction or retry on unique conflict. Two concurrent sync deliveries for the same user and app both observe no row and both insert. Later refreshes and calendar lookups also use findFirst without a stable order, so they can keep using a stale duplicate while the webhook updates a different row.

Zoom sync sends app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"

refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom credential is stored with appId "zoom" (see the OAuth callback) and the app-store slug used by the new webhook is "zoom". The parent app, which keys credentials by the slug it posted to /api/webhook/app-credential, will not find a "zoomvideo" credential. Zoom token refresh via the sync endpoint fails or refreshes the wrong app, while every other adapter in this PR passes its real app slug (google-calendar, msteams, office365-calendar, and so on).

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and silent

uniqueGuests keeps a guest unless guest === attendee.email and unless blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest). The blacklist entries are lowercased, but the input is not lowercased or trimmed, so BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is bypassed by changing case. The same address can also be stored twice (User@x.com vs user@x.com), and duplicates inside the guests array are not removed, so one request can insert the same attendee twice. Filtered addresses are dropped with no per-email error: if any other address remains, the handler returns success and the UI says guests were added; if every address is filtered out, the error is emails_must_be_unique_valid, which is wrong for a blacklist hit. Normalize before compare, dedupe the input, exclude the organizer address, and reject blocked emails instead of skipping them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check requires both roles

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner, so the caller must be both. That does not match the variable name or the bookings UI, which treats team admin and owner as alternative managers (isUserTeamAdminOrOwner). A team admin who is not an owner is always FORBIDDEN; if those helpers treat ADMIN and OWNER as distinct membership roles, owners are forbidden too. Team managers will see Add guests on a team booking and the mutation will reject them. Use ||, and do not call either helper with teamId 0 when eventType.teamId is null.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails use the raw guest list and hide send failures

sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the original guests input, not uniqueGuests. In email-manager, any attendee whose email is in that list gets AttendeeScheduledEmail (a new confirmation plus ICS REQUEST) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Re-submitting someone already on the booking therefore pushes a second confirmed invite to them, while addresses that were filtered out still affect that branch. The call is wrapped in a try/catch that only console.log's a static string and then returns { message: "Guests added" }, so the dialog shows success even when nobody was notified. Pass only the addresses actually inserted, and log or surface the real send error.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive and silent

uniqueGuests keeps a guest unless guest === attendee.email and unless blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest). The blacklist entries are lowercased, but the input is not lowercased or trimmed, so BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is bypassed by changing case. The same address can also be stored twice (User@x.com vs user@x.com), and duplicates inside the guests array are not removed, so one request can insert the same attendee twice. Filtered addresses are dropped with no per-email error: if any other address remains, the handler returns success and the UI says guests were added; if every address is filtered out, the error is emails_must_be_unique_valid, which is wrong for a blacklist hit. Normalize before compare, dedupe the input, exclude the organizer address, and reject blocked emails instead of skipping them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest mail ignores standard-email disable flags

sendLocationChangeEmails and the other send helpers in this file skip host or attendee mail when event-type metadata has disableStandardEmails. sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team.members entry, and every attendee, and addGuestsHandler never passes eventType.metadata. Event types configured to suppress standard emails still get guest-added messages and ICS attachments, bypassing workflow-only notification settings. Apply the same host and attendee disable checks here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar payload omits team, so co-hosts are skipped

The CalendarEvent built for updateCalendarAttendees and sendAddGuestsEmails never sets team. sendAddGuestsEmails only notifies other hosts when calendarEvent.team.members is present, so that loop is dead for this caller. Collective and round-robin co-hosts get no guest-added email or ICS, and destinationCalendar falls back to a single booking.user calendar, so their calendars are not updated either. Populate team the same way the other booking email builders do before calling EventManager and sendAddGuestsEmails.

Calendar update uses the actor and is not rolled back

Attendees are inserted with createMany before updateCalendarAttendees. The EventManager is then built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user), while booking.user (including credentials) was loaded and never used. If a team admin or attendee adds guests, the update targets that person's calendars, not the host calendar that owns the event, so the real event's attendee list is not updated or the call throws. The throw is outside any transaction and outside the email try/catch, so the mutation errors after the rows are committed. A retry then filters those emails as already present and fails with emails_must_be_unique_valid, leaving the booking, calendars, and notifications permanently out of sync. Use the booking host's credentials and roll back the insert if the calendar update fails.

Cancelled and rejected bookings can be re-invited

Nothing checks booking.status before creating attendees and sending mail. addGuests is only authedProcedure plus the handler's role check, so an organizer, attendee, or permitted team member can call it for a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking even though the list UI hides the action. The new organizer and attendee emails attach an ICS REQUEST with status CONFIRMED, which can put the meeting back on calendars and re-send the video link for a meeting that was declined or cancelled. Gate the update on ACCEPTED (or another explicit allow-list) before writing attendees.

Guest list has no maximum length

guests is z.array(z.string().email()) with no min or max. Anyone the handler allows, including any attendee on the booking, can submit thousands of addresses in one call. Each new address becomes an Attendee row, and sendAddGuestsEmails sends a full booking message (location and video link included) to every attendee. That is an unbounded write and a meeting-link spam path with no limit on this procedure. Cap the array in ZAddGuestsInputSchema and reject an empty list.

No tests for addGuests authorization or side effects

The new mutation decides who may add guests, how emails are filtered, and whether cancelled, seated, or disableGuests bookings are writable, but the PR adds no handler or router tests. The admin&&owner check, case-sensitive blacklist bypass, and cancelled-booking ICS path would ship unnoticed. Cover organizer, team admin, team owner, unrelated user, duplicate and blacklisted emails, seated event types, and non-ACCEPTED statuses.

Seated events ignore capacity and seat records

createMany inserts Attendee rows without checking seatsPerTimeSlot (the same handler later copies that field onto the calendar payload) and without creating BookingSeat rows. Seat availability and payment are based on seat count, so these extra attendees can exceed the cap, receive the meeting link without a paid seat, and are invisible to seat cancel/reschedule flows that use seatsReferences. The emails also include the full attendee list, which leaks other people when seatsShowAttendees is false. Reject addGuests for seated event types, or enforce remaining capacity and create the matching seat records.

disableGuests on the event type is ignored

eventType is included on the booking but disableGuests is never read. The normal booking flow refuses additional guests when that flag is set; this mutation still creates Attendee rows and emails them the meeting details. Because the permission check also allows any existing attendee, a guest on a no-guests event type can invite arbitrary people after the fact. Reject the request when booking.eventType.disableGuests is true.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount write is not atomic under overlapping crons

Both failure paths set retryCount to the in-memory reminder.retryCount + 1 (here and in the catch at line 195) instead of an atomic increment. The handler loops every due reminder with several queries and a Twilio call, and it is a cron POST that can be invoked again if the previous run is still going or the scheduler retries a timeout. Two runs read the same count, both can call scheduleSMS for the same unscheduled row, and both write the same retryCount, so the retryCount > 1 delete never observes the real number of attempts and does not stop duplicate sends. Use retryCount: { increment: 1 } and claim the row before calling Twilio so a second run cannot schedule it again.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes reminders this job does not own

The new deleteMany branch matches every WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 and does not require method SMS, scheduled false, or any scheduledDate bound. WorkflowReminder also stores EMAIL and WHATSAPP rows, and an SMS row can already be scheduled true with a Twilio referenceId if a later attempt succeeds or a concurrent run records success while another run has already bumped retryCount past 1. The next cron then deletes those rows. Email and WhatsApp reminders are dropped and never send. A scheduled SMS loses its referenceId without cancelling the provider message, so the text can still go out and can no longer be tracked or cancelled. The original delete was limited to SMS; that limit was not applied to this OR branch. Scope it to unscheduled SMS rows this job actually failed.

false_positives.candidate:
Broad catch burns the two-strike limit and can duplicate SMS

The catch surrounds template building, the organizer profile lookup, getBookerBaseUrl, twilio.scheduleSMS, and the success update that sets scheduled and referenceId. Any throw increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false. If Twilio already accepted the message and only the following update failed, the SID is discarded and the next cron calls scheduleSMS again, sending a duplicate; after two such errors retryCount is 2 and the opening deleteMany removes the row while those provider messages stay queued. The same path treats transient failures (DB blip, booker URL, empty attendees) as permanent send failures. This cron loads every unscheduled SMS in the next 7 days, so two errored passes delete that whole backlog and those bookings never get an SMS. Only count a retry when the provider rejects the send, and if scheduleSMS already returned a SID, persist that SID instead of incrementing.

Cleanup comment no longer describes the delete

The comment says this deletes scheduled SMS reminders whose scheduled date is already past. The query never filters on scheduled true, and the new OR branch also deletes any method's reminder with retryCount > 1, including future rows. Someone editing this later from the comment can restore or narrow the wrong predicate and either resurrect the infinite retry or keep deleting email and WhatsApp reminders.

Missing number or empty body is retried until the send date

retryCount is incremented only when message is non-empty and sendTo is set, and only if scheduleSMS returns a falsy value or throws. If the step has no sendTo, the booking has no smsReminderNumber, or the rendered body is empty, the loop just continues. The row stays scheduled false with retryCount 0 and is selected again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop (invalid or missing phone). Treat a missing destination or empty message as a terminal failure so those reminders are not loaded until the event date.

No tests for the retry limit or what gets deleted

This change deletes reminder rows and stops SMS after a small number of failures, and nothing in the PR covers that contract. Needed cases: one failure leaves the row and a second failure makes the next run delete it; the gt: 1 cutoff matches "failed twice" and does not allow a third scheduleSMS call; EMAIL and WHATSAPP rows with any retryCount are not deleted; a falsy scheduleSMS result and a thrown provider error both increment; empty sendTo or an empty body does not get reselected until the date; a successful schedule does not increment and is not deleted while still in the future. Without those, the unscoped OR and the two-strike catch can drop or duplicate reminders unnoticed.

retryCount delete is not covered by an index

deleteMany now ORs retryCount > 1 onto the cleanup, but WorkflowReminder only indexes (method, scheduled, scheduledDate), (bookingUid), (workflowStepId), (seatReferenceId), and (cancelled, scheduledDate). The new column in schema.prisma has no index. Postgres cannot serve that OR branch from the existing composite index, so every cron run can sequentially scan WorkflowReminder before any SMS is scheduled. That table grows with bookings; a slow cleanup makes this endpoint more likely to overlap the next cron tick.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
ANY(${number[]}) does not bind a Postgres array, so team/org auth queries fail

Org and team authorization interpolate JavaScript number arrays as Prisma.sql`"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds})` (same pattern at the team-scope user list). Prisma.sql binds each interpolated value as one query parameter; a JS array is not expanded into a PostgreSQL int[]. At execution this typically errors with operator does not exist: integer = text or malformed array literal (the parameter is sent as text/JSON like [1,2,3], not '{1,2,3}'::int[]). Team and org insights then throw instead of returning rows. The length > 0 guard avoids an empty list but does not fix binding. Use a form Prisma actually supports, such as "teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)}) or "teamId" = ANY(ARRAY[${Prisma.join(teamIds)}]::int[]), and keep the empty-list guard because Prisma.join([]) produces invalid IN (). The new tests never execute these statements: they deep-compare Sql objects, and the only $queryRaw case is user scope, which has no ANY().

Composed-condition assertions compare nested Sql objects to flat templates

Team scope (this expect), org scope, and the combined eventTypeId+memberUserId filter expect a single flat Prisma.sql`...` template. The service builds those predicates with reduce, nesting fragments (Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` / AND). Prisma stores nested Sql instances on .values and only flattens them when the query runs, so Vitest toEqual compares different .strings/.values and these tests fail even if the rendered SQL matches. The author noted the suite was not run. User-scope and single-filter expects happen to be one template on both sides and can pass while the composed authorization paths stay red and unexecuted. Assert rendered SQL (or execute team/org conditions with $queryRaw, including a row that must be excluded) instead of structural equality of differently built Sql objects.

Team/org auth SQL is an ungrouped OR, so extra AND filters skip team bookings

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition return a top-level OR, e.g. (("teamId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)), with no parentheses around the whole predicate. getBaseConditions returns that fragment unchanged whenever there is no eventTypeId/memberUserId filter (the common path; date bounds are not part of InsightsBookingServiceFilterOptions and must be applied by the caller). AND binds tighter than OR, so WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ${start} AND "startTime" < ${end} is parsed as (team-booking match) OR (personal-booking match AND date range). Every team booking for that team/org is returned with no time bound, and any other caller AND (event-type allow-list, status, extra auth) is likewise dropped for the team-booking side. The same trap exists on the public event-type filter at the ungrouped OR in buildFilterConditions ("eventTypeId" = $1 OR "eventParentId" = $1): WHERE auth AND that fragment becomes (auth AND eventTypeId = $1) OR eventParentId = $1, which can return rows outside authorization. getBaseConditions only parenthesizes when both auth and filters are present, and the tests assert the ungrouped form, so they do not catch this. Wrap every returned fragment in an outer (...) so it is one grouped predicate before it is embedded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty updateMany throws after every cache write

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) after upserting CalendarCache. Prisma Client rejects updateMany when data is an empty object ("Argument data needs at least one argument"), so this throws on every successful cache fill, including Google webhook refreshes and the refill at the end of unwatchCalendar. Callers that treat the throw as a sync/watch failure will retry, record errors, and can eventually stop watching the calendar even though the cache write already succeeded. An empty payload also does not reliably bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. The new repository method types data as SelectedCalendarUpdateInput, which is not assignable to updateMany's UpdateManyMutationInput. Pass an explicit update such as { updatedAt: new Date() }.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper fails on Linux and writes the wrong env file

The script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '', which is BSD/macOS sed and fails on GNU sed, so the env update does not work on Linux. ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the current working directory, not the script or repo root. Running bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repository root therefore targets a path outside the repo, and if that file is missing touch creates it and writes the tunnel URL there instead of the project .env. Resolve the env path from the script directory and use a portable in-place edit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deleting cache does not stop watches that recreate it

deleteCacheHandler only runs calendarCache.deleteMany for the credential. It does not clear Google channel fields or stop notification channels. Webhook handling calls fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache, which writes CalendarCache again, so for any watched Google calendar the rows return on the next push and the delete looks like it failed. The new confirm_delete_cache string says the action cannot be undone, which is false while watches are active. Either stop watches the way unwatchCalendar does before deleting, or tell the user the cache will be rebuilt and trigger a refetch. The access check also throws a plain Error, which tRPC reports as an internal 500 instead of NOT_FOUND or FORBIDDEN.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp format is a type error and ignores locale

The last-updated label always does new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }).format(new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)). cacheUpdatedAt is Date | null | undefined, and hasCache is a separate boolean, so TypeScript does not narrow it; new Date(cacheUpdatedAt) is not assignable under strictNullChecks and should fail typecheck. The formatter is also hardcoded to en-US, so the translated cache_last_updated string still shows a US timestamp for every locale. Format only a narrowed Date with the active locale.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache delete does not refresh connected calendars

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars (or apps.integrations). The calendar settings query lives in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper and onChanged is often omitted, so after a successful delete the dropdown still shows the previous Last updated time and the delete action. Users are told the cache was deleted while the UI keeps offering to delete it until a full reload.

Cache status counts expired rows as live cache

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups every CalendarCache row for the credential and takes max(updatedAt), with no expiresAt >= now filter. Availability reads ignore expired rows, but the settings dropdown treats any truthy cacheUpdatedAt as live cache and offers Delete cached data. Credentials whose cache has fully expired still show a last-updated time. Restrict the query to unexpired rows, and return no status when every row is expired.

Existing cache rows are stamped with migration time

updatedAt is added as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), so every existing CalendarCache row gets the migration execution time rather than the last free/busy write. The new status query uses max(updatedAt), so after deploy every Google credential that already has cache will show that deploy timestamp as Last updated until the next Prisma upsert. Backfill from a closer signal (for example expiresAt minus the cache TTL) or keep legacy updatedAt null and only display a timestamp after a real update.

No tests for cache delete authorization or status

deleteCache is a new mutation that deletes CalendarCache rows after an ownership check, and getCacheStatusByCredentialIds changes what connectedCalendars returns, but there are no unit or integration tests. A dropped userId filter, deleting another user's credential, or stale cacheUpdatedAt after delete would not be caught. Cover owner success, rejection of another user's credentialId, and that connected calendars no longer report cache after deletion.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget and can be dropped

On cancel, deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are started inside forEach and never awaited, and the handler returns after awaiting unrelated calendar/prisma work. The email path only persists WorkflowReminder.cancelled=true; it does not call SendGrid in this request. On a serverless API route the isolate can freeze before that update commits, so cancelled stays unset and the cron never cancels the batch. The same un-awaited forEach is used for reschedule in handleNewBooking.ts around line 966 (wrapped in a try/catch that cannot see async failures), requestReschedule in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx around line 488, and workflow delete/update in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx around lines 212, 376, 519, and 574. This PR removed the previously awaited workflowReminder deletes, so a dropped call now means the reminder email or SMS is still sent.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete cancels SendGrid and then forgets the row

When immediateDelete is true, deleteScheduledEmailReminder POSTs a SendGrid batch cancel and returns without setting cancelled=true or deleting the WorkflowReminder. Reschedule (handleNewBooking.ts) uses this flag, so a failed or dropped SendGrid call leaves an active scheduled row that the cron will not retry, because the cron only cancels rows with cancelled=true. Workflow and step deletion also pass true and then cascade-delete the rows, so a failed cancel cannot be retried either. Immediate cancels also occupy a SendGrid scheduled_sends slot until the original send time. That is the 100-pending-cancellation cap this PR is trying to avoid, and rescheduling far-future reminders reintroduces it on the path the PR claims to fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cron deletes cancelled reminders before cancelling them at SendGrid

The handler first deleteMany's every EMAIL WorkflowReminder whose scheduledDate is already in the past, including cancelled=true rows that were never cancelled at SendGrid. Only after that does it load cancelled reminders and POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends. The cron runs every 15 minutes and only attempts SendGrid cancel inside a one-hour window. If a run is skipped or the cancel loop throws while a cancelled reminder's send time elapses, the next run removes the row and leaves the SendGrid batch scheduled, so the reminder is still delivered. Past-due cancelled rows must be cancelled at SendGrid before deletion, and this deleteMany must exclude cancelled=true.

Deferred cancel still sends reminders due before the next cron tick

The non-immediate path only sets cancelled=true and waits for scheduleEmailReminders to POST the SendGrid cancel. That job runs every 15 minutes and only considers sends inside the next hour. A booking cancelled or rescheduled when the reminder is due sooner than the next cron run is still delivered, because nothing in the request calls SendGrid and there is no second chance once scheduledDate is in the past (those rows are deleted first). Sends already inside the cron interval need an immediate SendGrid cancel here; deferral is only safe for sends further out.

No tests for the deferred cancellation the last fix got wrong

This change replaces immediate SendGrid cancellation with a cancelled flag plus cron finalization, and it adds no tests. Nothing asserts that a cancelled reminder inside the next hour is cancelled at SendGrid and then deleted, that one SendGrid failure does not skip the rest, that past-due cancelled rows are not deleted before cancel, or that booking cancel and reschedule actually persist cancelled=true before the handler returns. The previous fix (#6991) shipped broken for this same production bug; this regression will not be caught.

One SendGrid cancel error aborts every other cancellation

The cancel loop awaits client.request for each reminder and only deletes WorkflowReminder rows after the whole loop. Any throw (missing referenceId, an already-sent or already-cancelled batch, or SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation limit) jumps to the catch, skips the rest of the list, and does not await the deletes already queued. Those in-flight deletes can also be dropped when the request ends. The next run loads the same rows. A single poison reminder therefore blocks cancellation of every other due reminder, and batches that were already cancelled are retried every 15 minutes, which can keep the account pinned at the cancellation cap. Each reminder needs its own try/catch, and its row should be deleted only after that reminder's cancel succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule returns before calendar and video cleanup

requestReschedule now uses bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) so it can await getCalendar, but forEach does not wait for those promises. The mutation marks the booking CANCELLED, sends the reschedule email, fires BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and resolves while calendar.deleteEvent and deleteMeeting may not have started. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was at least invoked before the handler continued. Now the first await yields before any provider call, and a serverless isolate can exit before the dynamic import finishes. Rejected imports or delete failures are unhandled rejections with no surrounding try/catch. Collect the work with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) and await both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting before sending email or returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Vital reschedule does not wait for calendar or video deletion

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) does not await its callbacks, and the try/catch around it cannot see rejections from them. getCalendar is now async, so calendar.deleteEvent is not even started until that import resolves, and neither deleteEvent nor deleteMeeting is awaited. Reschedule then sends the reschedule email and returns true while the external calendar event and video meeting may still exist. On serverless, the handler can be frozen after the response, so the cleanup often never runs and the old slot stays busy. Failures become unhandled promise rejections. Replace this with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) and await both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting inside the mapper.

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring cancel races calendar deletion against Promise.all

When cancelling all remaining instances of a recurring event, credentials are still walked with forEach(async), and this change added await getCalendar inside that callback before deleteEvent. forEach does not wait, and apiDeletes.push only happens after both awaits, so the later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) (around line 652) usually runs while apiDeletes still lacks these deletions — often before deleteEvent has been called at all. The non-recurring else branch just below was correctly rewritten to a for-loop that awaits getCalendar and pushes the delete promise before continuing; the recurring branch was not. The handler can therefore return success while series events remain on the external calendar and those times stay busy. Errors in the callback are unhandled rejections. Await Promise.all on the credential list (and on each deleteEvent) instead of forEach, and push the promises before awaiting them if they must be included in apiDeletes.

WipeMyCal reschedule does not wait for calendar or video deletion

The same forEach(async) pattern was introduced here when getCalendar became async. Array.forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, so the try/catch never observes getCalendar, deleteEvent, or deleteMeeting failures, and the function sends the reschedule email and returns true without waiting for those calls. Because the first await is now the dynamic app import, deletion is no longer even initiated before the handler continues. Serverless runtimes can freeze after the response and drop that work, leaving the cancelled event on the user's calendar and the slot blocked. Await Promise.all over a map, and await deleteEvent and deleteMeeting inside it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours recheck rejects valid slots whenever a host has more than one window

checkIfIsAvailable now runs for every isFixed host, and personal events, collective events, and round-robin fixed hosts are all marked isFixed. The new working-hours test uses Array.find and returns unavailable if the slot falls outside any single window whose days include the slot's UTC weekday. A host with a lunch break, or a single local range that getWorkingHours splits across UTC midnight into two entries on the same day, therefore fails the check for every slot: a 10:00 slot inside 09:00–12:00 is still outside 13:00–17:00, so find matches and the slot is dropped. The booking page then shows no times. The condition is also inverted for days off: if no window lists that weekday, find matches nothing and the host is treated as free, so a fixed host who does not work that day is not actually blocked. The end minute is copied from slot start (hour*60+minute of slotStartTime, not slot end), so a slot that starts inside a window but whose event length runs past endTime is accepted. Net effect is both false unavailability for ordinary split schedules and false availability outside hours.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date-override hit skips busy times and mishandles multiple or empty overrides

On a day that has a date override, if the slot is considered inside an override, checkIfIsAvailable sets dateOverrideExist and returns true immediately, before the busy/booking loop. A fixed host (including every personal or collective host) who blocked 15:00 with a calendar event or Cal booking, but has a date override covering that time, is reported free, so the slot stays bookable and can double-book. The same find() treats "outside this one override" as a hard unavailable: two override windows on the same day reject a slot that sits in only one of them, because the other window's callback returns true. Zero-length overrides (the unavailable-day convention, start equal to end) are detected with dayjs object ===, which is never true for two instances, so that branch never runs. Day matching compares dayjs(date.start).add(offset).format (process-local mode) to slotStartTime.format (UTC mode), so when the server TZ is not UTC the override is attached to the wrong calendar day or ignored. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it is not treated as outside, so it takes the early available return as well.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers fixed-host overrides or the new availability recheck

The only new test re-queries a personal event date override in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants as the IST case. It never builds a round-robin event with a fixed host, which is the main fix described in the PR, and it never hits checkIfIsAvailable's date-override or working-hours branches. Split working hours, an override day that also has a booking, an unavailable (start==end) override, and a timezone shift that crosses midnight are all untested, so the regressions above would merge green.

Override timezone shift uses Date.toString and drops times that cross midnight

Active date overrides are converted with dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone). Date.toString() is the process-local representation (and often includes a parenthetical zone name), so the parsed instant used for utcOffset is wrong or Invalid Date off UTC, and utcOffset becomes NaN. timeZone is optional on TimeRange; if it is missing, .tz(undefined) throws RangeError and getSlots fails for the whole day instead of falling back. The shifted clock time is then reduced with .hour() and .minute() only. Adding inviteeOffset-organizerOffset across midnight wraps to 0–24h on the unadjusted day (the activeOverrides filter still keys off the raw UTC start). When the wrapped end is less than the wrapped start, buildSlots drops the range (start >= end), so the override disappears. Attendees in a distant timezone see the override on the wrong date or not at all — the bug this change is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender lookup assumes metadata shape and 500s otherwise

After finding an ACTIVE Integration with no OrganizationIntegration, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. This pipeline never writes sender (build_integration only copies state["sender"], which nothing in the new flow sets), and older rows may not have that key or may store a non-dict. A missing or malformed sender raises KeyError/TypeError instead of the installation error page, so re-link/reinstall of those installations 500s and the security check never returns a controlled failure. The same block also re-fetches with status=ACTIVE and turns a non-active Integration into the generic authenticity error, which is a behavior change from the previous re-link path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Installer check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist yet

The new GitHub-user check is the point of this change, but GitHubInstallation only compares pipeline state github_authenticated_user to metadata sender after an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. If Integration.DoesNotExist — the normal case when the browser returns with installation_id before the installation webhook is processed, or if the webhook never arrives — dispatch calls pipeline.next_step() immediately. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user either, so the OAuth login is discarded. Any Sentry user who completes OAuth as themselves can still bind an arbitrary Sentry GitHub App installation_id (leaked or raced) to their organization and inherit that installation's repo access. The stated mismatch failure does not cover the path that actually creates the integration.

Not-found install test never reaches the GitHub 404 path

test_installation_not_found no longer starts a pipeline via init_path. It hits setup_path with only installation_id (no setup_action=install), which PipelineAdvancer treats as no pipeline and redirects to / with "Invalid request.", then issues a second request whose state (ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05) is not the pipeline signature used everywhere else (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3). That cannot exchange a code, cannot call the stubbed 404 installation endpoint, and cannot produce the old "The GitHub installation could not be found." error. The assertion was weakened to the generic authenticity string, so the 404 contract is untested and this test should fail or pass for the wrong reason.

Token exchange drops the redirect_uri used to obtain the code

OAuthLoginView always sends redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect (built at the redirect just above), but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. OAuth 2.0 requires that if redirect_uri was included in the authorization request, the token request must repeat that exact value; GitHub otherwise rejects the code with bad_verification_code or redirect_uri_mismatch. Every install then dies on the generic authenticity error after the user consents. The new tests stub the token endpoint and never assert the POST body, so they cannot catch this.

User-mismatch test signs the pre-mutation webhook body

test_github_user_mismatch loads INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE, sets sender.login to "attacker", then posts that modified JSON with the original hardcoded X-Hub-Signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486. The HMAC is over the raw body, so it cannot match after the mutation. If signature verification is on, the webhook is rejected, no Integration sender is stored, and the later check for "Invalid installation request." is the same string OAuthLoginView returns for a bad state — so the test does not prove the OAuth login was compared to the installing user. There is also no case where sender login matches the stubbed octocat user and an already-existing Integration is allowed to proceed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time

AssignmentSource.queued is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. Dataclass defaults are evaluated once when the class body is executed, not on each construction, and datetime is not a default_factory. Every AssignmentSource created via from_integration or from_dict without an explicit queued value therefore shares the single timestamp captured when the module was imported. The field is meant to record when that assignment change was queued and is copied into every outbound task payload via to_dict, but rapid successive assignee updates (the case this PR is fixing) are indistinguishable by time, and freeze_time in tests cannot affect it. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each source gets its own timestamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource dict is not a safe Celery payload

to_dict() is dataclasses.asdict, so the dict passed to sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async in sync_group_assignee_outbound includes queued as a raw datetime. That task previously accepted only ints, a bool, and None. A datetime is not JSON-serializable: under a JSON task serializer, apply_async raises TypeError while handling the inbound webhook, after GroupAssignee.assign/deassign has already written the assignee. The webhook then errors, linked integrations other than the source never get the update, and retries repeat the failure. from_dict is also not an inverse of to_dict: it splats the dict into the constructor and only catches TypeError/ValueError, so an ISO-string queued value is accepted as a str rather than parsed, and any malformed payload returns None. The outbound task treats None as "no source" and calls should_sync without a source, which re-enables the echo and brings the sync loop back. Eager task tests never cross this serialization boundary, so they do not catch it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Cross-integration and deassign cycle behavior untested

The new test only assigns with AssignmentSource.from_integration on the same integration that owns the single linked external issue and asserts sync_assignee_outbound is not called. Nothing covers a second linked integration with a different id, which is the case the change claims must still propagate, so a regression that skips every outbound sync whenever any AssignmentSource is present would still pass. Inbound deassign now also threads assignment_source through GroupAssignee.deassign, but the deassign test still only expects assignment_source=None and never asserts that a matching source suppresses the outbound unassign. Both paths are required to stop the Jira assignee loop.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Registered metric-alert handler is now uninstantiable

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler and implements none of its abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data). It is still assigned as MetricAlertFire.detector_handler, and Detector.detector_handler instantiates that class with no try/except. Any detector whose type slug is metric_alert_fire will raise TypeError inside process_detectors and abort the whole batch. Previously this handler was concrete and evaluate() returned an empty result, so the same detector was a no-op instead of a crash.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list

StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], and process_detectors depends on .values() of that dict. The docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, which will mislead callers that were updated for the signature change.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Occurrence test helper ignores the evaluated value, so the new hook is not actually checked

build_mock_occurrence_and_event accepts value but never uses it, and MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data just calls that helper. Every new assertion rebuilds the expected occurrence with the same helper, so a regression that drops or swaps the value argument still passes. The inputs already disagree with the expectations: test_state_results_multi_group feeds group_2=10 but expects an occurrence built with 6; TestEvaluate uses packet values 100 and 8 while expecting occurrences built with 6. Those tests therefore do not lock in the contract this PR adds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Occurrence context ignores the schedule_type display copy

get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config and, when schedule_type is present, replaces it with get_schedule_type_display() on that copy. The returned context then sets "config" to monitor_environment.monitor.config, the original dict, so the display conversion is discarded. Issue occurrences therefore publish the raw schedule_type integer (for example 0/1) instead of "crontab"/"interval". The returned dict is also the live in-memory config object, so any later mutation of the event context config mutates the cached monitor instance. Return the modified copy.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Incident opens without N consecutive failures

try_incident_threshold treats failure_issue_threshold as a lookback window, then opens an incident whenever none of those rows are CheckInStatus.OK. It never requires len(previous_checkins) >= failure_issue_threshold, and it does not require every row in the window to be a failure status (ERROR, MISSED, or TIMEOUT). A new monitor whose config asks for 3 consecutive failures still flips to ERROR and creates a MonitorIncident on the first failure, because the query returns one row and that row is not OK. A window such as [IN_PROGRESS, ERROR] with threshold 2 also opens an incident after a single real failure, since IN_PROGRESS is not OK. That creates issues and fires monitor_environment_failed before the configured consecutive-failure count is met. Require a full window of failure statuses before transitioning status and creating the incident.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard metric tags break tag parsing

shard_tag is a comma-joined list of every shard a process owns and is emitted as a metric tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce (key shard) and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce (key shards). DogStatsD, which sentry.utils.metrics uses, treats commas as tag separators, so a value like 0,1,2 is parsed as extra tags and the series is dropped or attributed to the wrong tags. With the new CLI default --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so this is the default path whenever a consumer has more than one partition. The value is also unique per partition assignment, so rebalances create a high-cardinality series. wait_produce uses the key shards while produce uses shard, so the two timers cannot be correlated. Emit a bounded process index, or one tag per shard, and use the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Drift wait is a no-op, so the flusher test stays racy

test_basic patches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to give the flusher thread time to observe current_drift after it is set to 9000. That call is the patched no-op, so it does not wait. step.join() immediately sets stopped, which can exit the flusher before it flushes, and (msg,) = messages then fails intermittently. The new multi-process test only checks process counts and never asserts that shards split across flushers are actually produced once. Patch sentry.spans.consumers.process.flusher.time.sleep instead of time.sleep, and wait until a message is produced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Drift wait is a no-op, so the flusher test stays racy

test_basic patches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to give the flusher thread time to observe current_drift after it is set to 9000. That call is the patched no-op, so it does not wait. step.join() immediately sets stopped, which can exit the flusher before it flushes, and (msg,) = messages then fails intermittently. The new multi-process test only checks process counts and never asserts that shards split across flushers are actually produced once. Patch sentry.spans.consumers.process.flusher.time.sleep instead of time.sleep, and wait until a message is produced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without force-stopping flusher processes

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped and then calls next_step.join with the full timeout. If that consumes the budget, remaining_time <= 0 and the loop breaks without process.terminate() for every flusher process. close() intentionally does not stop these processes (to avoid a Redis memory spike at the start of rebalance), so join is the only force-stop path. Arroyo calls join with a finite timeout on shutdown and rebalance, and the consumer process stays alive across rebalance, so an un-killed flusher keeps flushing shards this consumer no longer owns. Those segments race the new assignee and are produced again to the buffered-segments topic. The wait is also sequential, so one slow process can exhaust the deadline and skip terminate() for the rest. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. After signaling stop, join must terminate and reap every process even when the timeout is already spent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart overlaps two flushers on the same shards

_ensure_processes_alive SIGKILLs a hung flusher and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards without joining the old process. Process.kill() only sends the signal and returns, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, Kafka produce, or done_flush_segments while the replacement starts flushing the same shard list. Both then read and clear the same Redis segments and emit them to buffered-segments, duplicating downstream data, and they also race on the shared backpressure_since and healthy_since values. The old Process object is dropped without being reaped, so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits. The replacement must be started only after the previous process has actually exited.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block offset commits, but the assertion requires the partition to be absent from committed_offsets. The worker always complete_offset in a finally, including when the patched processor raises, so a commit of offset 102 (101+1) is the actual behavior and the assertion fails if it happens. The test only sleeps 0.2s after the calls return, while the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit, so the assertion usually passes only because the commit has not run yet and fails when scheduling is slower. It neither locks the intended contract nor reliably passes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
An exception in the worker finally kills the only thread for that queue forever

OrderedQueueWorker has no supervisor. complete_offset and metrics.gauge run in the same finally block with no handler, and run() has no outer try around the loop. If gauge (or complete_offset) raises, the thread exits. That queue is the only worker for every group hashed to it, and nothing restarts it. Any offset already queued there stays in outstanding forever, so get_committable_offsets cannot advance that partition. The consumer keeps polling, health checks still pass because poll() only records queue depth, and commits for the partition stop until the process is restarted.

Offsets are committed from a background thread against a non-thread-safe Kafka consumer

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback (and therefore the Kafka consumer's stage/commit path) every second. The consumer thread is simultaneously in poll()/submit(). confluent-kafka Consumer objects are not thread-safe, and Arroyo's commit policy mutates shared offset state that is only used from the processing thread elsewhere. Concurrent commit and poll can crash the consumer, skip commits, or publish a torn offset map. terminate() only sets shutdown_event and does not join this thread, so it can still be inside commit_function after the processor has closed the consumer. close() joins the thread for at most 5s and then continues, so a slow commit leaves two commit threads if a new strategy is created. Commit from poll() on the consumer thread instead.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but poll() only emits a gauge and never pauses the consumer. A slow subscription (the case this mode is meant to isolate) makes its queue retain every subsequent message in memory while the main thread keeps fetching. Offset commits cannot advance past that item, so the process holds the entire uncommitted backlog until it OOMs. get_committable_offsets also walks range(start, max_offset+1) under the partition lock, so a large backlog stalls every worker's complete_offset for the duration of that scan.

Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance and later messages are committed unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. Strategy.close() (queue_consumer.py) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets each worker's shutdown flag, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on every partition revoke/assign, so the next strategy is handed a pool whose queues reject puts and whose workers are dead. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit then hits the bare except, logs, and add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The commit thread treats that as success and commits offset+1. After the first rebalance or consumer restart-in-process, every uptime result is acknowledged and dropped. The same except also permanently drops any message whose grouping function or enqueue raises, instead of letting the consumer retry.

Shutdown abandons queued work and can block for num_queues * 5s

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run only calls get() while that flag is false. After the current item, the worker exits even if Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) would still return queued items, so those items are never processed and never completed. close() stops and joins the commit thread before joining workers, so items that do finish during shutdown are not committed either. join() ignores its timeout and calls close(). On a deploy/rebalance, in-flight uptime results are redelivered and applied twice (duplicate incidents/occurrences). Joins are also sequential with a 5s timeout each, so 20 workers stuck in slow handlers make close()/terminate() block for about 100s and still drop the work.

Uptime --mode help still describes the wrong execution model

uptime_options() now accepts thread-queue-parallel, but the help text is still "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." The parallel mode uses a multiprocessing pool, batched-parallel uses a thread pool, and thread-queue-parallel uses one thread per queue. Operators enabling the new flag get no description of what it does or that --max-workers is the queue count rather than a thread-pool size.

Worker threads never reset Django DB connections, so one DB error drops later results

OrderedQueueWorker calls result_processor on a long-lived thread and never calls django.db.close_old_connections(). Django only runs connection health checks and obsolete-connection cleanup on the request path, which these threads do not have. After an idle timeout, failover, or OperationalError, that thread's connection stays dead. ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows the exception, and the worker's finally still complete_offset, so the failed check is committed and will not be retried. Every later message on that same queue fails the same way and is also acknowledged. One transient DB blip silently disables 1/num_queues of subscription processing until the consumer restarts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every newly denied resource reloads the full permission set

If the permission cache hits but checkPermission is false, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions, which ignores the cache and loads every scope for that user and action from the DB, then writes the cache back. Absence in a just-refreshed complete set is treated the same as a stale cache. Denial entries only dedupe the exact same name and folder, so a sequential sweep of unauthorized resources (list filtering, many GETs) issues one full permission query per resource per 30s instead of the previous single query per user+action. Concurrent checks share one singleflight, but sequential checks do not.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test still denies if the cache is ignored

TestService_CacheCheck's explicit-deny case comments that the permission cache allows dash1 so a denial hit is the only way to deny, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no grant, and the fake permission store is empty, so a fall-through to the DB also returns Allowed=false. The test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed and does not cover deny-then-grant, renderer/anonymous key collision, or UID delimiter collisions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key joins name and folder with an underscore

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with '_' and no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and parent is often empty, so distinct resources share one key. For example name=foo, parent=bar and name=foo_bar, parent="" both become ..._foo_bar_, and name=abc, parent=de_f matches name=abc_de, parent=f. A deny for one resource then returns Allowed=false for the other for 30s with no permission or folder check.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type and collides on id 0

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID only, not the identity type or the canonical UID from GetUserIdentifiers. Anonymous checks use subject anonymous:0 and the renderer uses render:0 (both covered by tests), so both produce the same key for a given namespace, action, name, and folder. An anonymous deny of dashboards:read on a dashboard is then served to the renderer for 30s, and every anonymous retry refreshes that TTL, so image rendering/PDF of that dashboard can stay broken as long as anonymous checks keep missing. The reverse is also true for actions the renderer is denied. Numeric subjects (user:123) are likewise keyed separately from the resolved UID, so the same person does not share denial entries across id and uid forms, and a numeric id can collide with another identity whose id string matches.

Denial cache pins false denies and skips the DB re-query

Check returns Allowed=false as soon as permDenialCache has an entry for (namespace, subject id, action, name, parent), before reading permissions or the folder tree. That entry is written for every DB deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes it when permissions are granted or the folder cache is refreshed. A check that races ahead of the creator ACL insert (or any deny followed by a grant, including a new wildcard/admin role) therefore stays denied for the full TTL even though the new re-query path would now allow it. The same stickiness freezes inheritance failures caused by a stale folder tree: once denied, later requests never rebuild the tree or reload scopes. A slow in-flight query that snapshotted pre-grant rows can also Set the denial after a concurrent request already observed the grant, so retries keep failing for 30s. This recreates the 'creator cannot open what they just created' failure on the retry that the PR is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key

The grafana branch of the filtered-rule map used to render GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem has no key, while the datasource and unknown branches still use key. As infinite scroll appends rows, React can reuse the wrong list-item instance, so action-menu and drawer state can attach to a different rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item does not open a drawer

AlertRuleMenu shows Silence when the Prometheus-rule ability allows it and calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). The new list never passes a ruler rule, so clicking Silence notifications does nothing. The group-loader test only checks that the menu item exists and never clicks it.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating and deleting rules are no longer distinguished

GrafanaGroupLoader used to match ruler and Prometheus rules and render ruler-only rules as Creating and Prometheus-only rules as Deleting (without edit or more actions). It now lists only Prometheus rules. Until Prometheus catches up, a just-created rule is missing from the group, and a just-deleted rule still appears as a normal rule with edit, silence, duplicate, and export. The tests that covered those states were removed rather than replaced.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and block update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (TODO on line 243). Every caller of useAlertRuleAbility, including the existing rules UI, will offer edit and delete on Mimir/enterprise federated groups. groupIdentifier does not carry source_tenants, so the check was dropped rather than moved.

Pause and delete never appear without a ruler rule

The list view now computes canPause and canDelete from Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the menu still renders Pause only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123) and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165). GrafanaRuleListItem and FilterView pass only promRule, so both items stay hidden even for users who are allowed to pause or delete. Those actions are gone from the new alert list; GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx locks this in by expecting exactly four menu items and never asserting Delete or Pause.

Prometheus abilities treat only alerting rules as exportable

useAllRulerRuleAbilities allows ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently for any Grafana-managed rule (alerting or recording) via rulerRuleType.grafana.rule. useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates those same actions on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule. The list view relies on the Prometheus hook, so Grafana recording rules lose Export (and would also lose pause/restore/permanent delete once those menu items no longer require a ruler rule).

Rule links no longer include returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail back link returned to the current list, including filters. The new href is only /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view. Opening a rule from the list and using the in-app back control drops the user on the default alerting page instead of the filtered list.

isProvisionedPromRule reads provenance on a type that lacks it

isProvisionedPromRule takes PromRuleDTO and accesses promRule.provenance after prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule). That helper is not a type predicate, and PromRuleDTO (PromAlertingRuleDTO | PromRecordingRuleDTO) does not declare provenance — only GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase does. This is a TypeScript error, and RuleActionsButtons passes a Rule into this function, so provisioned detection for the clone flow may not typecheck. At runtime a non-Grafana rule short-circuits, but a Grafana rule is only treated as provisioned if the object happens to have provenance.

skipToken still grants Duplicate via Grafana create permission

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) evaluates useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) instead of returning all-denied abilities. With no rule, loading is false, so MaybeSupported is AlwaysSupported and Duplicate is allowed whenever the user has Grafana AlertingRuleCreate. AlertRuleMenu ORs that result with the ruler result, so cloud and ruler-only rules show Duplicate for anyone who can create Grafana rules, even when the datasource ability denies it. Update and Delete do not leak because their allowed flag stays false, but Duplicate does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Early interpolation defeats the $__range split exclusion

runSplitQuery now runs every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper replaces Grafana range macros ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from request.scopedVars using the full request range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on the already-rewritten expr, so the $__range token is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split because the macro is meant to be interpolated on the backend against each request's own time range. After this change each chunk is executed with the full-range duration baked in (for example count_over_time({app="x"}[7d]) on every 1-day slice), so merged results overlap or over-count and Loki load grows with the selected range. The new tests only cover $__auto and $step, and the default test templateSrv does not expand $__range, so this production path is untested.
