Interpolate only after classifying queries on the raw expr, and leave $__range* in the expression sent to the backend.

Shard queries are template-interpolated twice, including ad-hoc filters

runShardSplitQuery now maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters), then splitQueriesByStreamShard rewrites those expressions with interpolateShardingSelector and calls runSplitQuery. runSplitQuery unconditionally applies applyTemplateVariables again on that rewritten expr, with the same request.filters still set. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: ad-hoc filters are inserted into the stream selector on each call, so a sharded query gets duplicate matchers (or a failed/misplaced insertion once `| drop __stream_shard__` is already in the LogQL). A second template replace can also expand `$` sequences that appeared in variable values. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (once here plus once per split group) and only uses an idempotent replace mock, so it locks in the double application instead of catching duplicate filters. Interpolate once, before shard selector injection, and do not run applyTemplateVariables again inside runSplitQuery for targets that are already interpolated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs lose traceID

"Plugin Request Completed" used to include traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), so every valid trace (sampled or not) was on the log line. That field was removed and is not added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware, which only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname. The new call is logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) and Info does not take a context.Context, so the infra logger cannot recover the span at log time. Plugin request logs can no longer be correlated with traces, including unsampled ones that metrics exemplars (requireSampled=true) never recorded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs

LoggerMiddleware now emits the completion line via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...). TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a different object whose InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs are not the instance tests hold. Calls, message, and key/value pairs are silently dropped, so assertions on the injected test logger see zero logs even when a request was logged. The fake also ignores ctx, so it cannot observe the contextual attributes this change depends on.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
No test locks the moved contextual log fields

Contextual attributes were moved out of the metrics middleware into instrumentContext, and completion logs now depend on a separate middleware having called log.WithContextualAttributes before LoggerMiddleware.FromContext. Nothing in this change asserts that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics attach endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, or that "Plugin Request Completed" still emits them (and traceID). The renamed metrics test only checks Prometheus counters. A middleware reorder, a FromContext miss, or a dropped field would ship unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or unique cap. Concurrent anonymous logins that all observe count < deviceLimit all take the INSERT path and the table (and thus anonymous access) exceeds the configured limit. This is the common case when many new devices arrive together at the cap. The count and the insert/update need to be serialized (single transaction with a lock, or an insert that rechecks the cap) so the limit cannot be overrun.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached as success

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the 29-minute local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. On ErrDeviceLimitReached the first call correctly fails, but the cache entry is left in place and the next TagDevice for that same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache and returns nil. Authenticate treats nil as success, so anonymous access is granted and the device is never recorded. A client that retries once (or any later request within the TTL) bypasses the limit entirely. The cache is also not cleared on transient DB errors, so a failed write is treated as tagged and is not retried for 29 minutes. Set the cache only after a successful write, and do not treat a limit failure as a cache hit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is enforced only if the client sends a device id

The new auth denial depends on TagDevice, which returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and Authenticate then issues an anonymous identity. The header is optional and client-controlled, so omitting it never consumes a slot and never hits ErrDeviceLimitReached. A caller can also mint device_limit distinct ids to fill the quota (locking out honest frontends that do send the header) and then drop the header to keep its own anonymous access. As written, the limit cannot cap anonymous access. Enforcement needs a server-issued identifier, or requests without a tracked device must be denied once the cap is reached.

Device-limit failure is returned as an unclassified error

When the cap is hit, Authenticate returns the raw anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached sentinel (a plain fmt.Errorf). That is not an errutil or authn error, so the auth middleware treats it as an unexpected failure and typically responds with HTTP 500 rather than a controlled 401/403 and a user-facing device-limit message. It also shows up as a server error in logs. Return a typed unauthorized/forbidden auth error so the client chain and HTTP layer handle it as an access denial.

Limit tests miss the allow-existing path and auth enforcement

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts a second, unknown device id against the store and expects ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once the cap is reached, and nothing covers TagDevice, the local cache, or Anonymous.Authenticate. Those are the paths that actually grant or deny access, so the cache-as-success bypass and the missing-header bypass are untested and would ship green.

Provider signature change will not compile with existing wire code

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer accepts anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. This package is constructed by the committed Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR and still calls the old signatures. The server build fails until wire is regenerated. Any other in-repo or enterprise caller that passed an AnonStore is also broken, and tests can no longer inject a fake store.

device_limit is not added to default config

auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0), but conf/defaults.ini (and the docs generated from it) are not updated. Operators have no documented default, comment, or sample for the new cap, and 0-means-unlimited exists only in the store's if deviceLimit > 0 check. Add the key to the [auth.anonymous] section in defaults.ini with that meaning spelled out.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup debug logs left at Error level and dump every ID

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log every batch with r.log.Error, including the full ID slice, the SQL condition, and a nil err (same pattern at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). These run on the normal cleanup path, including the orphan-tag pass that always executes and the empty-batch case that happens when there is nothing to delete. Each scheduled cleanup will therefore emit error-level logs even when healthy, and when retention is configured a batch can be tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, inflates error metrics/alerts, and can stall or OOM the cleanup job while formatting the slice. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup scheduler interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1

CleanUpService.Run now ticks every 1 minute instead of 10, and the PR does not mention this. clean() is synchronous and its context timeout is 9 minutes, so the old interval left a gap between runs. With a 1-minute ticker, any cleanup that lasts longer than a minute (the timeout allows up to 9) finds a tick already pending and starts the next pass immediately, so temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, annotation, invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup can run back-to-back. That is a large unintended load increase and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix; restore the 10-minute interval.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). That copies the whole growing string on each ID. The new path is specifically for large batches (the test uses 32767, and the setting can be set higher), so one DELETE builds O(n^2) bytes of temporary strings — several seconds and heavy GC at 32k IDs, and much worse if the batch size is raised further. Build the list with strings.Builder (or strings.Join of preformatted IDs) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage and legacy durations are recorded on the wrong series

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration for a unified-storage failure, and Update does the same at line 129 with recordLegacyDuration. DeleteCollection's async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration, so the legacy outcome is counted as another storage observation and legacy delete-collection latency is never recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage failures to legacy and hide real legacy delete-collection failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful delete records the object name as the kind label

On a successful Storage.Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as the third argument. Every other call in this file passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, every distinct deleted name becomes a new series. That grows without bound for the process registry and any scraper, and the delete latency/error series can no longer be aggregated by kind.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). When the apiserver handler returns, that parent context is cancelled, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never applies, and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection observe context.Canceled instead of finishing. Mode 3's legacy copy therefore does not land on the success path, so a rollback to legacy storage loses or stale-reads every write that was acknowledged from unified storage.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection do not track their goroutines. Shutdown can destroy legacy storage while a goroutine is still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which races with teardown and drops the safety copy for writes that were already acknowledged. There is no WaitGroup or drain anywhere in DualWriterMode3.

Legacy update no longer persists the unified result

Update now passes the original objInfo into Legacy.Update after Storage.Update returns. The previous implementation computed the object once from unified storage and wrote that exact result to legacy through updateWrapper. In mode 3 the client resourceVersion comes from unified storage, so legacy GuaranteedUpdate's optimistic check fails with a conflict once the two backends' resource versions differ, and the safety copy is dropped. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, UpdatedObject runs against legacy's own old object and can persist a different spec. objInfo is also not guaranteed to be reusable after the first Update, so the async second call can fail or write a mutated object.

Legacy write failures are not logged

The async Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, and Legacy.DeleteCollection calls only feed a boolean into the duration metric. The previous synchronous path logged the legacy error with the object identity. A timeout, conflict, or context cancellation now leaves unified storage and legacy diverged with no log line, so the safety copy can fail indefinitely without an operator-visible signal.

Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the legacy write

Success-path tests install legacy On expectations (Create around line 31, Update around line 313) but return as soon as the synchronous unified call finishes, and they never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. testify will not fail if the legacy call is skipped, and the goroutine can invoke the mock after the test has finished. Both stores also share one mock.Mock, so a single Create/Update expectation cannot prove which backend ran. The new cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (file mode 3 at line 132, unified mode 3 at line 191) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets the legacy playlist API after a k8s write. Those checks assume the legacy write is synchronous; with this mode 3 they race, and they fail outright if the request context cancels the legacy write.

NotFound on unified delete skips legacy cleanup

Delete returns on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous mode 3 delete still removed the object from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. During migration, legacy can still hold objects that unified storage does not. Those deletes now fail to the client and leave the legacy row in place, so a fallback to legacy resurrects objects the API reported as gone.

Per-object legacy writes are unordered

Each successful Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection fires an independent goroutine with no per-key queue, lock, or generation check. The handler returns as soon as unified storage succeeds, so a later delete (or newer update) can be applied to legacy before the earlier create/update. Legacy can then contain a resurrected object or an older spec while unified storage, which mode 3 reads, has the new state. Rollback or any legacy reader then serves data the API already deleted or overwrote. The closure also shares the request object with the caller; if Storage.Create returns that same pointer, the caller's continued use races with Legacy.Create.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache and can clobber a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock and later takes the write lock without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that observed a nil cache (or is running in Dev) therefore reloads the manifest while holding the global mutex, then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. On a cold start, N concurrent calls all pass the nil check, queue on the write lock, and each performs a full file read; a later caller whose read fails stores nil and wipes the successful cache published by an earlier caller, so subsequent non-Dev requests miss and can return an error even though a valid asset set was already loaded. Re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock (and do not overwrite a non-nil cache with a failed load). The exclusive lock is also held across the manifest read, so those redundant loads are fully serialized.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache and can clobber a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock and later takes the write lock without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that observed a nil cache (or is running in Dev) therefore reloads the manifest while holding the global mutex, then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. On a cold start, N concurrent calls all pass the nil check, queue on the write lock, and each performs a full file read; a later caller whose read fails stores nil and wipes the successful cache published by an earlier caller, so subsequent non-Dev requests miss and can return an error even though a valid asset set was already loaded. Re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock (and do not overwrite a non-nil cache with a failed load). The exclusive lock is also held across the manifest read, so those redundant loads are fully serialized.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL disable helper inverts the feature flag and always returns false

enableSqlExpressions sets enabled to the negation of FlagSqlExpressions, then returns false whether that value is true or false, so the flag read does nothing. ReadQuery treats false as a hard error, so this reader disables SQL only because both branches hardcode false. The negation is the opposite of a normal allow-check, and nothing names CVE-2024-9264. The obvious edit to make the flag check meaningful (return true when the flag is on) would build SQL commands again on any instance with the still-documented sqlExpressions flag enabled. Make the disable unconditional and independent of the feature flag.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Disabled SQL expressions are reported as unimplemented or invalid SQL

When SQL expressions are refused, ReadQuery returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is wrong: the feature existed and is being turned off for CVE-2024-9264, not left unimplemented. On the expression command path, NewSQLCommand still returns the public BadRequest "error reading SQL command" (sql-invalid-sql in pkg/expr/sql_command.go) for every SQL expression, because TablesList now always fails. Users and support will treat a security disable as a syntax error in their query. Return one stable message that SQL expressions are disabled.

Live SQL path still interpolates user SQL into a DuckDB statement

TablesList still escape-doubles single quotes only and builds SELECT json_serialize_sql('<user SQL>'), then passes that string to RunCommands. NewSQLCommand calls TablesList for every SQL expression, and SQLCommand.Execute still forwards the raw query to QueryFramesInto. The new enableSqlExpressions check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery does not cover that path; the reader comment says it has not replaced the existing expression pipeline in transform.go. RunCommands and QueryFramesInto currently return "not implemented", so DuckDB is not invoked and this is not an active RCE. The CVE sink is still on the request path: quote-doubling does not make that statement safe, and any change that makes those methods succeed, or a caller that ignores the TablesList error and still executes, runs attacker-controlled SQL with no feature-flag gate. Reject in NewSQLCommand and Execute before formatting or dispatching SQL, and remove the json_serialize_sql interpolation.

No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected and not executed

This change is the CVE-2024-9264 fix (DuckDB removed, SQL expressions disabled) but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that a SQL expression fails closed on the production command path, that user SQL is not handed to an engine, or that turning on FlagSqlExpressions cannot restore execution. The mitigation is a stub whose methods return "not implemented"; restoring a real RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, or skipping the TablesList error and still calling Execute, would not fail CI. Add a test that builds a SQL expression through NewSQLCommand/Execute and expects a disable error without running the statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer single-flights per key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which also blocked GetIndex and serialized builders. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key]. getOrCreateIndex is still check-then-act (GetIndex, and on nil call build/BuildIndex) and has no per-key lock or singleflight. Concurrent first searches, watch events, or init workers for the same NamespacedResource therefore build two bleve indexes. The later cache write blindly overwrites the earlier one, so one caller keeps writing and searching an index that is no longer in the cache while everyone else uses the other. The discarded index is never closed (memory and file-handle leak). For file indexes both builders use the same directory, so the second bleve.New fails and that caller gets an error even if the first build succeeded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
File indexes cannot be reopened, so eager init crash-loops

When size exceeds FileThreshold, BuildIndex always calls bleve.New on a stable path (Root/namespace/resource.group) and never bleve.Open. bleve.New fails if that directory already exists. A successful build, a killed process, or a failed init that already created the directory leaves the path on disk. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any BuildIndex error aborts server construction, so the next start hits the same bleve.New error and the process cannot boot until the directory is deleted by hand. The removed log was the only hint that an existing index/RV should be reused; the TODO remains unimplemented.

Index init workers race on shared err

searchSupport.init starts initWorkers goroutines that all do `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and `return err`, plus `totalBatchesIndexed++`, on variables owned by the outer function with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race. One worker can return another worker's nil and hide a failed namespace build, so startup continues after an index failed (the opposite of the comment that any init failure must block startup), or a success can be overwritten and fail startup incorrectly. The span attribute namespaced_indexed is also racy. This function is now on the blocking startup path.

Postgres storage-server startup test is skipped

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for the storage-server target coming up and serving /metrics. This change makes NewResourceServer run unified-storage Init (stats, index build, watch) during that startup, which this test previously never reached because it never issued a storage RPC. The PR skips the test on postgres with a TODO that it fails in Drone, so the CI job that would catch a postgres-specific eager-init failure no longer runs it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test cleans up the wrong IdP alias

testCacheIDPForLogin creates providers with aliases idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-20, but every cleanup is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (the loop at line 381 and idp-alias-20 at line 425). The admin-client get() receiver is bound immediately, so cleanup DELETEs the nonexistent alias "alias" and never removes the providers this test created. Those IdPs remain in the shared realm. The test asserts exact cache sizes (5, 6, 10, 11), so a rerun, or testCacheIDPByOrg running first (it has the same get("alias") cleanup and leaves public org-idp-* brokers linked to orga), changes those counts and can fail this test or later organization tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses the org-aware isEnabled wrapper

update() loads the previous provider with getById() and passes that object into registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate. With the organization feature on, getById() does not return the stored model: it returns an anonymous IdentityProviderModel whose isEnabled() is false when the IdP is linked to an organization that is missing, disabled, or whose OrganizationProvider is disabled, even if the IdP's own enabled flag is still true. LoginFilter.ENABLED is IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled, so getLoginPredicate() fails for that wrapper. The method then returns without registering any .idp.login.* invalidation when both sides fail the predicate. That is exactly the in-session path (getByAlias/getById, mutate, update) while the org is disabled, and it also happens for an admin update whose raw model no longer qualifies (hide-on-login, link-only, enabled=false, kc.org.broker.public cleared, or organizationId moved) if the wrapped original already fails the predicate. The cached id set keeps the old membership until expiry. After the organization is enabled again, getForLogin still serves that set, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login, link-only, or broker-public. IdPs that were configured to stay off the login page, including non-public organization brokers, can be offered for login. Compare the delegate/raw model (and null-check it) instead of the organization-aware wrapper.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

The CryptoProvider contract says getBouncyCastleProvider returns the non-FIPS or FIPS BouncyCastle provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform provider for the default keystore type (typically SUN), not BC or BCFIPS. Callers use that Provider's name and instance for Cipher/Signature/CertificateFactory and for BouncyIntegration. Algorithms that exist only under BC (AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, many JOSE/JWE transforms, BCFKS) will fail or silently run outside FIPS when this provider is the one CryptoIntegration selected. Elytron returns null rather than a lookalike; this should not hand back an unrelated JCA provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Existing downstream or custom implementations (and any already-compiled class) will not have this method. ServiceLoader instantiates every provider and then calls order() during sort, so one old implementation on the classpath throws AbstractMethodError and aborts detection entirely, even if a newer provider is also present. That turns a compatible server startup into a hard failure. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep old providers loadable and still let the new order-200 providers win.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient.create can permanently install the stub crypto provider

AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init with AuthzClient's own classloader, and init only selects a provider when the static cryptoProvider field is still null. That selection is process-wide and never refreshed. AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services and implements almost every CryptoProvider method by throwing UnsupportedOperationException, with order 100. If create() runs before the server calls init with a classloader that can see DefaultCryptoProvider or FIPS1402Provider (deployment/module classloader that only exposes the authz-client service file, embedded startup, or a test that builds an AuthzClient first), the stub is locked in for the JVM. Later server init is a no-op, so token signing, PEM handling, and the other crypto entry points fail or use the incomplete provider even though a real one is on the server classpath.

ECDSA test does not compile in this module

ECDSAAlgorithmTest imports org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm and org.keycloak.crypto.JavaAlgorithm. Those types live in the server SPI (the crypto modules already import them from there), not in keycloak-core. authz/client/pom.xml only adds junit and hamcrest; its compile/test classpath is still just keycloak-core plus HTTP/Jackson. server-spi is not a dependency, and keycloak-core cannot depend on server-spi without a cycle. testCompile of keycloak-authz-client-tests therefore fails with a missing org.keycloak.crypto package, so the new coverage never runs.

ECDSA transcoding test never checks a real signature

The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip each other. The key pair is generated once with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC"), which is P-256 on standard JDKs, and that same key is used for ES256, ES384, and ES512. ES384/ES512 signature lengths are 96 and 132 bytes and their DER SEQUENCEs need long-form lengths once R and S match P-384/P-521, but a P-256 signature stays short and is only zero-padded to those lengths. Nothing calls Signature.verify on the original DER or on the re-encoded DER, and there is no known-answer vector. A self-consistent but non-interoperable encoder (wrong tag, non-minimal INTEGER, broken long-form length) still passes, which is the failure mode this provider exists to prevent.

Equal-order crypto providers are now chosen silently

detectProvider used to fail fast when ServiceLoader found more than one CryptoProvider. It now sorts by order() and keeps the first, only logging the rest. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so a classpath that contains both FIPS and non-FIPS (or Elytron and default) no longer errors. ServiceLoader order is classpath order, and sorted() is stable, so which full provider wins is environment-dependent. ServiceLoader also instantiates every provider before the sort, so FIPS1402Provider still inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE and rewrites key/trust manager security properties even if the non-FIPS provider is the one selected (and DefaultCryptoProvider still registers BouncyCastle). A FIPS deployment can therefore keep running in a mixed or non-FIPS mode instead of refusing to start. Tie at the winning order should still be a hard error, and FIPS must outrank the non-FIPS providers if silent preference is intended.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal listener checks V1 but dispatches V2 clients

Cleanup now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws. If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls the throwing V2 method and client deletion fails. If only V2 is on, the listener does nothing, so the authorization resource created for that client id is never removed. There is no other V2 delete hook in this change, so object-level client permissions are left pointing at deleted clients.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the type name, not client ids

getClientsWithPermission adds resource.getName() for every Clients-typed resource that grants the scope. The schema's all-clients resource is named "Clients" (init sets both name and type to the resource type). A user who only has a type-level grant therefore gets a set containing the literal "Clients" rather than every client id, and callers that filter with client.getId() match nothing. Object resources are only included if their type was set to Clients; getOrCreateResource creates them by name and scopes and never calls setType, so per-client grants are also omitted if no other layer sets the type. Listing and role-mapping UIs that rely on this set will hide clients the user is allowed to access. The type resource should be expanded or skipped, and returned ids must be real client ids.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing Clients resource NPEs permission checks

When no per-client resource exists, hasPermission assigns getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with no null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null if the "Clients" resource was never created. findByResource dereferences that resource and throws NullPointerException, so canView/canManage/canConfigure/canMapRoles return 500 instead of false. AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null and never adds the new Clients resource type or the new scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). Any realm that enabled admin permissions before this schema change keeps the old resource server, so the first per-client check 500s and creating a Clients permission fails because those scopes are absent. init needs an upgrade path, and the evaluator must treat a missing type resource as deny.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 throws on token exchange and permissions API

MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() now always returns ClientPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, but canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, mapRolesClientScopePermission, mapRolesCompositePermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, and getPermissions all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Token exchange calls AdminPermissions.management().clients().canExchangeTo and will fail the request with a server error for every realm that has the feature enabled, even if token-exchange permissions are unused. The admin client management-permissions endpoint calls isPermissionsEnabled, then resource and getPermissions, so opening fine-grained permissions for a client 500s. These methods are still part of the live ClientPermissions contract; they need a V2 behavior (or a safe deny/empty result), not an exception. getEvaluationContext is unused dead code left from an unfinished exchange check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Client permission resources have no display name

getResourceName only resolves Users resources to a username. Client object resources are stored under the client UUID (resolveClient returns client.getId()) and getOrCreateResource never sets a display name, so the fallback resource.getDisplayName() is null. Admin APIs that label permission resources will show a blank name for every client permission, and a deleted client is not reported as missing the way a missing user is (ModelIllegalStateException). This method needs a Clients branch that loads the client and returns its clientId, and a defined error if the client is gone.

Per-client resource hides all-clients allow and deny

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads the object resource by client id and, if that row exists, evaluates only that resource. The all-clients resource is consulted only when no object resource exists. Creating any object permission (for example VIEW on one client) therefore drops realm-wide grants such as MANAGE/CONFIGURE/MAP_ROLES on "Clients" for that client, so an admin who can manage every client loses manage on any client that also has an object-level permission. The same short-circuit skips a realm-wide negative permission, so a deny-all policy on Clients does not apply to a client that already has an object resource and a positive object permission. Authorization becomes order-dependent and can both lock out legitimate admins and bypass a type-level deny.

Role-mapping checks ignore manage-clients admins

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission and never treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS as sufficient. This class fully replaces ClientPermissions whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and V1 granted those operations to holders of manage-clients (including master-realm and realm admins) before any fine-grained policy was consulted. canManage and canManageClientScopes still short-circuit on that role, so the same admin can update a client but is denied mapping client roles, composite roles, and client-scope roles. Admin console role-mapping calls fail with 403 even when no FGAP policy was meant to restrict that admin. The new tests only cover a user without manage-clients, so they do not catch this.

requireView javadoc describes a boolean result

requireView is void and throws ForbiddenException, but its new javadoc says it returns true if canView() returns true. requireViewClientScopes (line 101) has the same error: it says it returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true. Callers reading the interface will treat these as predicates instead of enforcing methods. The comments should match requireManage/requireList and state that they throw when the corresponding can* check is false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Default-strategy upgrade tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, so spec.features.enabled is left unset for the null cases of testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount. Those cases still call deployKeycloak(..., true), which waits until the CR is ready, and then assert an upgrade status. The operator guide added in this PR says that while the feature is preview it must be enabled or the Operator will fail, including for the default <not set> strategy that mimics 26.1. As written, the default-strategy tests do not meet that precondition and will time out if the warning is true. If they pass, the warning is false and tells every operator user to turn on a preview feature or expect a failed reconcile. Enable the feature for every parameter value, and append it to any features already on the CR instead of setEnabledFeatures(List.of(...)) replacing the whole list, or narrow the caution if the default path is intentionally exempt.

Exit code 4 is documented as a failed rolling-upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says exit 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because rolling-updates is disabled. That is the same lead-in as exit 3, which means the deployment must be shut down before the new config is applied. The implementation does not evaluate compatibility in this case: UpdateCompatibilityCheck and UpdateCompatibilityMetadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and return FEATURE_DISABLED before any metadata is read. The guide tells automation to rely on these codes. Describing 4 as a negative compatibility result will cause pipelines to recreate or drain the cluster when the only required action is to enable the feature and rerun the check.

Recreate exit code moved from 4 to 3 and 4 reused

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3, and 4 is now FEATURE_DISABLED. update-compatibility is invoked as a separate process, so callers branch on the numeric code, not this Java constant; recompiling in-repo Java does not update them. This PR does not change any operator production code that runs the check, and UpdateCommandDistTest never asserts an exit code: testFeatureNotEnabled only checks stderr text, and testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility message. A caller still treating 4 as "incompatible, shut the cluster down first" will now take that path when the preview feature is merely off, and will not treat a real incompatibility (now exit 3) as recreate. That is the decision this tool exists to make; getting it backwards is either an unnecessary outage or a rolling update across incompatible versions. Lock both codes in the dist test and update every numeric comparison in the same change.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW permission is treated as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, so a caller who only has the Groups VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. requireManage() is the gate for creating top-level groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup). That caller can therefore create groups despite having only view access. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE, so the no-arg check is inconsistent with per-group enforcement and with the security model. The interface javadoc repeats the same VIEW-or-MANAGE rule and should be corrected with the implementation.

This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() walks resources with findByType and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). hasPermission treats its argument as a group id and looks the resource up with findByName. Instance group resources are named with the group id (resolveGroup returns group.getId()), while Resource.getId() is the authorization resource primary key, so the lookup misses the group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource. The id added to the set is also not a group id. UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource put that set on the session as UserModel.GROUPS and pass it to getUsersCount. A non-empty set of authz ids makes user search and counts match no real groups (admins with view-members see nobody). The all-groups type resource itself is included by findByType; if it has view-members, its internal id is added and poisons the same filter. The set should contain resource names that are actual group ids, and the type resource named "Groups" must be skipped. Current tests still pass when the set stays empty because listing post-filters with canView, so they do not catch a wrong or empty id set on the count/search path.

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else reconciles the schema. Realms that enabled fine-grained admin permissions before this change keep a resource server that has no Groups type resource and no manage-membership, manage-members, or view-members scopes. Creating a group permission then hits getOrCreateResource, which throws ModelException("No scopes found.") when a schema scope is missing. Evaluations that fall back to getResourceTypeResource("Groups") get null, and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission calls policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() on that null, turning a missing schema into a 500 instead of a deny.

getOrCreateResource creates the instance resource with resourceStore.create and updates scopes, but never calls setType(resourceType). The schema init path does set type on the type-level resources, which shows create() does not infer it. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission depends on resourceStore.findByType(..., GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Group resources created for fine-grained permissions therefore are not returned, so view-members and manage-members grants on specific groups are invisible to user search and user-count filtering.

getResourceName special-cases only the Users type and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group instance resources are created with the group id as the name and no display name, and this change never adds a Groups branch that loads the group and returns its name or path. Permission listings for the new Groups resource type therefore show null (or a raw id) instead of a group name, and a missing group is not reported the way a missing user is.

AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and the GroupRemovedEvent listener still calls groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is also enabled. Deleting a group then fails the listener with UnsupportedOperationException and can roll back the delete. The same throw hits the group management/permissions admin endpoints, which still require the V1 feature and then call these methods. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all, so deleting a group leaves its authorization resources and policies behind with no V2 cleanup.

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers is false. Callers reading only the contract will enforce or test membership management instead of member management.

A null rawTokenId is stored. encodeTokenId then concatenates it, and Java string conversion turns that into the literal suffix "null" (for example onrtac:null). Every such token shares the same jti, so revocation, event correlation, and replay checks that key on token ID collapse together. The check must be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...).

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token ID matcher rejects a matching grant and checks the wrong slice

isAccessTokenId is what the updated CODE_TO_TOKEN, refresh, device, and CIBA event assertions now use, but matchesSafely is inverted and off by one. Encoded IDs are six characters before the colon: session type at 0-1, token type at 2-3, grant type at 4-5 (for example onrtac:<uuid>). The check uses substring(3, 5), which is the last character of the token-type shortcut plus the first character of the grant shortcut, and returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For a correct ID the wrong slice does not equal the expected shortcut, so the method falls through and only checks that the suffix looks like a UUID. Integration tests therefore pass for any <prefix>:<uuid>, including a wrong grant shortcut or the na fallback, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters also throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException out of the matcher instead of failing the match. The condition needs to require a 6-character prefix and compare substring(4, 6) to the expected shortcut.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not constrained to 2 unique characters, so issued IDs cannot be decoded

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() is documented as "usually like 3-letters", but the encoder writes the shortcut as-is and getTokenContextFromTokenId requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2+2+2) and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise. postInit stores whatever getShortcut() returns and only compares map sizes, so a 1-character, 3-character, empty, or colon-containing shortcut still starts the server and is embedded in new access-token IDs. Those tokens cannot be parsed by the same provider. The lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType (around line 113) and getGrantTypeByShortcut is worse: on a cache miss it puts the new shortcut into both maps with no length check and no uniqueness check, so a hot-deployed grant can overwrite another grant's shortcut. Decoding then either throws or reports the wrong grant type. Validate at registration and on the lazy path that every shortcut is exactly two characters, contains no ':', and is not already mapped to a different grant; fix the javadoc to match.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Decode error claims the whole token ID must be length 6

When the prefix before ':' is not 6 characters, the exception says Incorrect token id: '<full id>'. Expected length of 6. The full jti is a 6-character prefix plus ':' plus a UUID, so the message describes the wrong length and will send operators looking at the wrong field when decode starts failing requests.

New getShortcut() method breaks existing grant factories at startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing SPI, and getShortcut() was added as an abstract method with no default. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit casts every OAuth2GrantType factory and calls getShortcut() while building the shortcut maps. A custom grant factory compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError during that postInit, which aborts Keycloak startup rather than only disabling that grant. Add a default implementation and treat a missing or null shortcut as unknown so already-deployed grant providers keep the server bootable.

Unset grant type is silently encoded as na on issuance paths this PR did not update

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext treats a missing ClientSessionContext Constants.GRANT_TYPE attribute as the shortcut na, and encodeTokenId will persist that into the access-token jti. This PR only sets the attribute in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, the ROPC and pre-authorized grants, StandardTokenExchangeProvider, and the refresh path in TokenManager.validateToken. Other callers of TokenManager.initToken / createClientAccessToken are unchanged. Implicit and hybrid access tokens are issued from the authorization endpoint, not the token endpoint, and legacy token-exchange providers other than StandardTokenExchangeProvider are not in this diff. Those tokens are minted with grant shortcut na even though the grant is known. Once introspection or session lookup trusts the encoded grant (the stated reason for this change), those tokens take the unknown-grant path and the optimization is wrong. Every access-token issuance path needs to set the real grant, or initToken must fail instead of writing na for a request whose grant is known.

Reference user storage accepts any recovery code forever and stores them in plaintext

Without a restart they stay undeployed, so the new browser-flow execution and CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action do not run createRecoveryCodesCredential. After credentialManager().isValid succeeds, this authenticator assumes the credential row was already updated and, when allCodesUsed() is true, deletes it with removeStoredCredentialById. That side effect exists only in the local recovery-code credential provider. For the new user-storage path, isValid is delegated to the storage provider and this method never writes the remaining codes back with updateCredential. removeStoredCredentialById only deletes credentials stored in Keycloak's database, not credentials owned by user storage, and the id on a federated model is not a local credential id. A correct storage that marks codes used therefore leaves an exhausted credential in place: isConfiguredFor stays true, the browser flow keeps challenging for a recovery code before required actions run, and the user is locked out once the last code is consumed. A storage that does not mutate state on isValid (as the new test provider does) leaves every code reusable forever, and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES action is never added.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard metric tags break tag parsing

shard_tag is a comma-joined list of every shard a process owns and is emitted as a metric tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce (key shard) and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce (key shards). DogStatsD, which sentry.utils.metrics uses, treats commas as tag separators, so a value like 0,1,2 is parsed as extra tags and the series is dropped or attributed to the wrong tags. With the new CLI default --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so this is the default path whenever a consumer has more than one partition. The value is also unique per partition assignment, so rebalances create a high-cardinality series. wait_produce uses the key shards while produce uses shard, so the two timers cannot be correlated. Emit a bounded process index, or one tag per shard, and use the same key.

Although the candidate also raises additional concerns about comma-joined values in DogStatsD, it clearly captures the target issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without force-stopping flusher processes

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped and then calls next_step.join with the full timeout. If that consumes the budget, remaining_time <= 0 and the loop breaks without process.terminate() for every flusher process. close() intentionally does not stop these processes (to avoid a Redis memory spike at the start of rebalance), so join is the only force-stop path. Arroyo calls join with a finite timeout on shutdown and rebalance, and the consumer process stays alive across rebalance, so an un-killed flusher keeps flushing shards this consumer no longer owns. Those segments race the new assignee and are produced again to the buffered-segments topic. The wait is also sequential, so one slow process can exhaust the deadline and skip terminate() for the rest. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. After signaling stop, join must terminate and reap every process even when the timeout is already spent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop in `join` when the timeout/deadline is exceeded causes remaining flusher processes to not be terminated, leaving them running.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart overlaps two flushers on the same shards

The old Process object is dropped without being reaped, so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits. The replacement must be started only after the previous process has actually exited.

false_positives.candidate:
Suspect-issue PR comments call methods that do not exist on the workflow

get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, but _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration, not on PRCommentWorkflow. PRCommentWorkflow is a separate workflow type that holds an integration; it does not gain that staticmethod. GitHubPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body also call self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template and self.get_environment_info, which were added only on CommitContextIntegration. Generating a merged-PR suspect-issue comment therefore raises AttributeError and the GitHub/GitLab comment workflow fails instead of posting.

Issue titles are interpolated into markdown links unsanitized

MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE places the issue title inside a markdown link label: [**{title}**]({url}). Issue titles are attacker-controlled error text and are only length-truncated, not escaped. A title containing ](https://evil.example) or a newline closes the link early and can inject extra markdown into the comment the Sentry bot posts on the customer's GitHub/GitLab PR. Environment names are likewise dropped into the comment in backticks with no escaping.

Replay error lookup depends on date filters the client never sends

Every summarize request now calls get_filter_params and query_replay_instance before building logs, and process_raw_response is given request.query_params.getlist('field'). The replay AI tab requests /summarize/breadcrumbs/ with no start, end, statsPeriod, or field=error_ids. If get_filter_params rejects a missing range, the previously working summary 400s. If it defaults to a recent window, error_ids is empty for replays outside that window, so error context is silently omitted. A Snuba failure also 500s a path that previously only needed recording segments. error_ids must be requested explicitly and the replay's own time range used, not the caller's page filters.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the search filter branch. When searchQuery is empty the function returns sortAttributes(attributes) immediately, so those internal fields stay visible in the default attributes tree. They disappear only after the user types a query, including when the query would otherwise match them. The exclusion needs to run before the early return.

Feedback summary ignores environment (and search) page filters

useFeedbackSummary requests /feedback-summary/ with only the normalized datetime and selection.projects. The feedback list page is scoped by the page-filter environment selection (and the search box), but those are not sent. With an environment selected, the Seer summary describes all environments in the projects while the list shows one environment, so the summary does not match the data on screen.

Feedback list no longer fills the grid cell and will not scroll

The list grid area used to be a FluidHeight Container, which constrained height and scrolled the list inside the 1fr row. It is now SummaryListContainer, a flex column with no min-height: 0, overflow: hidden, or height: 100%. Grid items default to min-height: auto, so the column grows with the summary plus the full list instead of staying in the viewport row, and the inner FluidHeight percentage height does not resolve to the leftover space. The feedback list scroll pane breaks once the summary is shown.

Attribute key hook returns undefined after a failed fetch

The old hook always reduced the response into a TagCollection, so a failed request still yielded {}. The new hook returns useQuery data directly (attributes: isFetching ? previous : data) and dropped retry: false. On error, data is undefined and isFetching is false, so attributes becomes undefined. Explore callers that spread or index attributes (string tags, number tags, has-tag) will throw when the trace-item attributes endpoint fails. Default react-query retry (3) and refetchOnWindowFocus also replace the previous retry: false and refetchOnWindowFocus: false, multiplying load on that endpoint.

60s deadline is too short for a 100-identity SSO refresh batch

check_auth_identities now has processing_deadline_duration=60 while check_auth still hands it up to chunk_size (100) identities. Each identity can do an external IdP refresh. check_auth stamps last_synced before enqueueing this task, so if the worker kills the task at 60s the remaining identities are not refreshed and will not be selected again until the next AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL (about a day). SSO validity checks are skipped for the tail of every oversized batch.

AI summary treats an unloaded project as missing

Project is resolved with useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id}), which is undefined both while the project list is still loading and when the project truly does not exist. The new branch returns 'Project not found' whenever project_id is set and project is missing, before the isPending check, and the summarize query stays disabled. Users hit a hard error (at least a flash, or a stuck error if projects never include that id yet) instead of waiting for the project store.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW permission is treated as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, so a caller who only has the Groups VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. requireManage() is the gate for creating top-level groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup). That caller can therefore create groups despite having only view access. canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE, so the no-arg check is inconsistent with per-group enforcement and with the security model. The interface javadoc repeats the same VIEW-or-MANAGE rule and should be corrected with the implementation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() improperly includes the VIEW scope in its hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) check, allowing users with only VIEW permissions to pass the manage check and gain unintended write/management access.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group view filter stores authz resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() walks resources with findByType and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). hasPermission treats its argument as a group id and looks the resource up with findByName. Instance group resources are named with the group id (resolveGroup returns group.getId()), while Resource.getId() is the authorization resource primary key, so the lookup misses the group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource. The id added to the set is also not a group id. UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource put that set on the session as UserModel.GROUPS and pass it to getUsersCount. A non-empty set of authz ids makes user search and counts match no real groups (admins with view-members see nobody). The all-groups type resource itself is included by findByType; if it has view-members, its internal id is added and poisons the same filter. The set should contain resource names that are actual group ids, and the type resource named "Groups" must be skipped. Current tests still pass when the set stays empty because listing post-filters with canView, so they do not catch a wrong or empty id set on the count/search path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`: using `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource ID) instead of the resource name (which stores the actual group ID) when calling `hasPermission` and adding to `granted`. Both note that `hasPermission` looks up resources by name, causing a mismatch and fallback to the 'all-groups' resource, and that the resulting IDs are misused in `UserModel.GROUPS` and `getUsersCount` filters.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-group authz resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource creates the instance resource with resourceStore.create and updates scopes, but never calls setType(resourceType). The schema init path does set type on the type-level resources, which shows create() does not infer it. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission depends on resourceStore.findByType(..., GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Group resources created for fine-grained permissions therefore are not returned, so view-members and manage-members grants on specific groups are invisible to user search and user-count filtering.

Existing admin-permissions clients never gain Groups scopes

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else reconciles the schema. Realms that enabled fine-grained admin permissions before this change keep a resource server that has no Groups type resource and no manage-membership, manage-members, or view-members scopes. Creating a group permission then hits getOrCreateResource, which throws ModelException("No scopes found.") when a schema scope is missing. Evaluations that fall back to getResourceTypeResource("Groups") get null, and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission calls policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes() on that null, turning a missing schema into a 500 instead of a deny.

V2 group permission management throws and breaks group deletion

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (and isPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions, and the policy accessors) always throw UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and the GroupRemovedEvent listener still calls groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is also enabled. Deleting a group then fails the listener with UnsupportedOperationException and can roll back the delete. The same throw hits the group management/permissions admin endpoints, which still require the V1 feature and then call these methods. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is not registered at all, so deleting a group leaves its authorization resources and policies behind with no V2 cleanup.

Permission resource names are not resolved for groups

getResourceName special-cases only the Users type and otherwise returns resource.getDisplayName(). Group instance resources are created with the group id as the name and no display name, and this change never adds a Groups branch that loads the group and returns its name or path. Permission listings for the new Groups resource type therefore show null (or a raw id) instead of a group name, and a missing group is not reported the way a missing user is.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers is false. Callers reading only the contract will enforce or test membership management instead of member management.
