false_positives.candidate:
Account UI message switched to Java MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the account-ui bundle was changed from i18next placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}) to Java MessageFormat, including a ChoiceFormat fragment {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}. Every other string in this file uses {{ }} interpolation, and the account console translates with i18next, not MessageFormat. The validation error will show literal {0}/{1} and the choice pattern instead of the attribute name and limits. The embedded <values token can also be parsed as a tag if the string is rendered through i18next Trans, which this theme already uses for strings such as <0>{{username}}</0>.

Admin UI message switched to Java MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the admin-ui (keycloak.v2) bundle was changed from Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s). to a Java ChoiceFormat string. This file is consumed by the React admin console via i18next, which only interpolates {{ }} placeholders. Users will see the raw {0}, {1}, and {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values} text, so the multivalued-size validation error no longer names the attribute or the limits. The Java MessageFormat version belongs only in the server theme bundles under themes/src/main/resources.

Lithuanian login loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian

loginTotpStep1 in the Lithuanian login bundle was replaced with the Italian sentence "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:". The previous value was Lithuanian. On the OTP setup page, lt locale users will see Italian instead of a translation of the English "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:".

Illegal-HTML diff trim can throw and abort the build

When sanitized text differs from the message, the reporter trims a shared prefix (start) and shared suffix (end) and then calls value.substring(start, value.length() - end) and the same on sanitized. The loops do not stop when the two regions overlap, so start can be greater than length - end. That throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. A concrete case is value "aaa" and sanitized "aaaa" (or any insertion/deletion inside a run of identical characters): start and end both become 3 and substring(3, 0) throws. The exception is unchecked and is not turned into a messages entry, so the Maven plugin aborts with a stack trace and never reports which key had illegal HTML.

Anchor mismatch message omits key and file

When a translated anchor does not exactly match the English anchor, the verifier only records "Didn't find anchor tag " + the tag + " in original string". Unlike the illegal-HTML message, this includes neither the message key nor the properties path. The theme verifier scans every locale file; a CI failure then does not say which file or key introduced the href, so the anchor check cannot be acted on without rerunning under a debugger.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-checks grantType twice and allows a null raw token ID

The fourth Objects.requireNonNull call passes grantType again, with the message "Null rawTokenId not allowed", instead of checking rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId is stored. encodeTokenId then concatenates it, and Java string conversion turns that into the literal suffix "null" (for example onrtac:null). Every such token shares the same jti, so revocation, event correlation, and replay checks that key on token ID collapse together. The check must be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the fourth Objects.requireNonNull call in the constructor validates grantType a second time instead of rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token ID matcher rejects a matching grant and checks the wrong slice

isAccessTokenId is what the updated CODE_TO_TOKEN, refresh, device, and CIBA event assertions now use, but matchesSafely is inverted and off by one. Encoded IDs are six characters before the colon: session type at 0-1, token type at 2-3, grant type at 4-5 (for example onrtac:<uuid>). The check uses substring(3, 5), which is the last character of the token-type shortcut plus the first character of the grant shortcut, and returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut. For a correct ID the wrong slice does not equal the expected shortcut, so the method falls through and only checks that the suffix looks like a UUID. Integration tests therefore pass for any <prefix>:<uuid>, including a wrong grant shortcut or the na fallback, and they never check session type or token type. A prefix shorter than 5 characters also throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException out of the matcher instead of failing the match. The condition needs to require a 6-character prefix and compare substring(4, 6) to the expected shortcut.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same two bugs in `isAccessTokenId`: the substring indices are off by one (should be `substring(4, 6)` for indices 4-5) and the equality check logic is inverted (returning `false` on a match instead of `true`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not constrained to 2 unique characters, so issued IDs cannot be decoded

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() is documented as "usually like 3-letters", but the encoder writes the shortcut as-is and getTokenContextFromTokenId requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2+2+2) and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise. postInit stores whatever getShortcut() returns and only compares map sizes, so a 1-character, 3-character, empty, or colon-containing shortcut still starts the server and is embedded in new access-token IDs. Those tokens cannot be parsed by the same provider. The lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType (around line 113) and getGrantTypeByShortcut is worse: on a cache miss it puts the new shortcut into both maps with no length check and no uniqueness check, so a hot-deployed grant can overwrite another grant's shortcut. Decoding then either throws or reports the wrong grant type. Validate at registration and on the lazy path that every shortcut is exactly two characters, contains no ':', and is not already mapped to a different grant; fix the javadoc to match.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment points out a discrepancy where the Javadoc for `getShortcut()` mentions 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', whereas the actual implementation uses 2-letter shortcuts. The candidate issue explicitly identifies this exact same Javadoc discrepancy ('OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() is documented as "usually like 3-letters"... fix the javadoc to match' the 2-character requirement) while also expanding on the runtime validation issues if non-2-letter shortcuts are used.

false_positives.candidate:
New getShortcut() method breaks existing grant factories at startup

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing SPI, and getShortcut() was added as an abstract method with no default. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit casts every OAuth2GrantType factory and calls getShortcut() while building the shortcut maps. A custom grant factory compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError during that postInit, which aborts Keycloak startup rather than only disabling that grant. Add a default implementation and treat a missing or null shortcut as unknown so already-deployed grant providers keep the server bootable.

Unset grant type is silently encoded as na on issuance paths this PR did not update

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext treats a missing ClientSessionContext Constants.GRANT_TYPE attribute as the shortcut na, and encodeTokenId will persist that into the access-token jti. This PR only sets the attribute in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, the ROPC and pre-authorized grants, StandardTokenExchangeProvider, and the refresh path in TokenManager.validateToken. Other callers of TokenManager.initToken / createClientAccessToken are unchanged. Implicit and hybrid access tokens are issued from the authorization endpoint, not the token endpoint, and legacy token-exchange providers other than StandardTokenExchangeProvider are not in this diff. Those tokens are minted with grant shortcut na even though the grant is known. Once introspection or session lookup trusts the encoded grant (the stated reason for this change), those tokens take the unknown-grant path and the optimization is wrong. Every access-token issuance path needs to set the real grant, or initToken must fail instead of writing na for a request whose grant is known.

Decode error claims the whole token ID must be length 6

When the prefix before ':' is not 6 characters, the exception says Incorrect token id: '<full id>'. Expected length of 6. The full jti is a 6-character prefix plus ':' plus a UUID, so the message describes the wrong length and will send operators looking at the wrong field when decode starts failing requests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recovery-code login form throws if the federated credential is missing or incomplete

The constructor always calls credentialModelOpt.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel, then getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get(). getCredential now prefers getFederatedCredentialsStream() over local storage. If that stream is empty (storage accepted updateCredential but does not implement getCredentials), if the model has no secretData, or if every code is already used, rendering the recovery-code page throws NoSuchElementException or a JSON error instead of a challenge. Previously this bean only read local credentials created by the credential provider, which always had the hashed schema and a remaining code when the form was shown.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment specifically identifies calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent(), which leads to a NoSuchElementException. The candidate issue points out the exact same bug: calling credentialModelOpt.get() unconditionally on the result of getCredential, which throws a NoSuchElementException if the stream is empty.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reference user storage accepts any recovery code forever and stores them in plaintext

updateCredential saves input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim in credentialData, which is the JSON array of raw codes, not hashes. isValid then returns true if any stored code equals the input and does not remove the match or require it to be the next unused code. getCredentials ignores that stored model and calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues on the original list, which assigns a new id and marks every code unused. So the code index shown at login never advances, allCodesUsed() is never true, removeStoredCredentialById cannot target the real id, and a captured code can be replayed indefinitely. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only signs in once with code 0, so it does not catch replay, a stuck index, plaintext persistence, or failure to force regeneration.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact problem described in the golden comment: that creating a new `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `createFromValues` does not preserve the stored credential ID, which means `removeStoredCredentialById cannot target the real id`. Although the candidate bundles this with other related flaws in the reference implementation, it clearly captures the target issue.

false_positives.candidate:
User-storage write payload cannot be read back as a recovery-code credential

createRecoveryCodesCredential tells user storage to persist only a JSON array of the raw recovery codes (UserCredentialModel challenge response). It drops generatedAt, the user label, and the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel that createFromValues already built. RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator then take the first federated credential of this type and pass it to RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel, which requires secretData in Keycloak's hashed schema. A provider that stores the updateCredential value and returns that CredentialModel (secretData null, credentialData = the raw JSON) — the same shape this PR's test storage saves, and the same pattern used for OTP — makes the login form throw while parsing, or throws after isValid already accepted the code, so recovery-code login never completes. Only the test provider papers over this by ignoring the stored model and calling createFromValues inside getCredentials.

Used federated recovery codes are not consumed or deleted

After credentialManager().isValid succeeds, this authenticator assumes the credential row was already updated and, when allCodesUsed() is true, deletes it with removeStoredCredentialById. That side effect exists only in the local recovery-code credential provider. For the new user-storage path, isValid is delegated to the storage provider and this method never writes the remaining codes back with updateCredential. removeStoredCredentialById only deletes credentials stored in Keycloak's database, not credentials owned by user storage, and the id on a federated model is not a local credential id. A correct storage that marks codes used therefore leaves an exhausted credential in place: isConfiguredFor stays true, the browser flow keeps challenging for a recovery code before required actions run, and the user is locked out once the last code is consumed. A storage that does not mutate state on isValid (as the new test provider does) leaves every code reusable forever, and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES action is never added.

Recovery-codes feature is enabled without restarting the server

@EnableFeature(RECOVERY_CODES, skipRestart = true) only flips the runtime profile flag. RecoveryAuthnCodesAction, the recovery-authn-codes credential provider, and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticatorFactory are environment-dependent factories whose isSupported() checks that feature and which are registered at server start. Without a restart they stay undeployed, so the new browser-flow execution and CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action do not run createRecoveryCodesCredential. The test can fail or not exercise the user-storage path at all. Omit skipRestart so the server restarts with the providers loaded.

Recreate exit code moved from 4 to 3 and 4 reused

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3, and 4 is now FEATURE_DISABLED. update-compatibility is invoked as a separate process, so callers branch on the numeric code, not this Java constant; recompiling in-repo Java does not update them. This PR does not change any operator production code that runs the check, and UpdateCommandDistTest never asserts an exit code: testFeatureNotEnabled only checks stderr text, and testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility message. A caller still treating 4 as "incompatible, shut the cluster down first" will now take that path when the preview feature is merely off, and will not treat a real incompatibility (now exit 3) as recreate. That is the decision this tool exists to make; getting it backwards is either an unnecessary outage or a rolling update across incompatible versions. Lock both codes in the dist test and update every numeric comparison in the same change.

Exit code 4 is documented as a failed rolling-upgrade decision

The new exit-code row says exit 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because rolling-updates is disabled. That is the same lead-in as exit 3, which means the deployment must be shut down before the new config is applied. The implementation does not evaluate compatibility in this case: UpdateCompatibilityCheck and UpdateCompatibilityMetadata print "Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled." and return FEATURE_DISABLED before any metadata is read. The guide tells automation to rely on these codes. Describing 4 as a negative compatibility result will cause pipelines to recreate or drain the cluster when the only required action is to enable the feature and rerun the check.

Default-strategy upgrade tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, so spec.features.enabled is left unset for the null cases of testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount. Those cases still call deployKeycloak(..., true), which waits until the CR is ready, and then assert an upgrade status. The operator guide added in this PR says that while the feature is preview it must be enabled or the Operator will fail, including for the default <not set> strategy that mimics 26.1. As written, the default-strategy tests do not meet that precondition and will time out if the warning is true. If they pass, the warning is false and tells every operator user to turn on a preview feature or expect a failed reconcile. Enable the feature for every parameter value, and append it to any features already on the CR instead of setEnabledFeatures(List.of(...)) replacing the whole list, or narrow the caution if the default path is intentionally exempt.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time

AssignmentSource.queued is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. Dataclass defaults are evaluated once when the class body is executed, not on each construction, and datetime is not a default_factory. Every AssignmentSource created via from_integration or from_dict without an explicit queued value therefore shares the single timestamp captured when the module was imported. The field is meant to record when that assignment change was queued and is copied into every outbound task payload via to_dict, but rapid successive assignee updates (the case this PR is fixing) are indistinguishable by time, and freeze_time in tests cannot affect it. The webhook then errors, linked integrations other than the source never get the update, and retries repeat the failure. from_dict is also not an inverse of to_dict: it splats the dict into the constructor and only catches TypeError/ValueError, so an ISO-string queued value is accepted as a str rather than parsed, and any malformed payload returns None. true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and races the commit loop

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block offset commits, but the assertion requires the partition to be absent from committed_offsets. The worker always complete_offset in a finally, including when the patched processor raises, so a commit of offset 102 (101+1) is the actual behavior and the assertion fails if it happens. The test only sleeps 0.2s after the calls return, while the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit, so the assertion usually passes only because the commit has not run yet and fails when scheduling is slower. It neither locks the intended contract nor reliably passes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts the opposite of its docstring, directly matching the golden comment's concern that the docstring doesn't match the test implementation, and provides further detail on why.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance and later messages are committed unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. Strategy.close() (queue_consumer.py) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets each worker's shutdown flag, calls Queue.shutdown(), and joins the workers. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on every partition revoke/assign, so the next strategy is handed a pool whose queues reject puts and whose workers are dead. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit then hits the bare except, logs, and add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The commit thread treats that as success and commits offset+1. After the first rebalance or consumer restart-in-process, every uptime result is acknowledged and dropped. The same except also permanently drops any message whose grouping function or enqueue raises, instead of letting the consumer retry.

Offsets are committed from a background thread against a non-thread-safe Kafka consumer

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback (and therefore the Kafka consumer's stage/commit path) every second. The consumer thread is simultaneously in poll()/submit(). confluent-kafka Consumer objects are not thread-safe, and Arroyo's commit policy mutates shared offset state that is only used from the processing thread elsewhere. Concurrent commit and poll can crash the consumer, skip commits, or publish a torn offset map. terminate() only sets shutdown_event and does not join this thread, so it can still be inside commit_function after the processor has closed the consumer. close() joins the thread for at most 5s and then continues, so a slow commit leaves two commit threads if a new strategy is created. Commit from poll() on the consumer thread instead.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but poll() only emits a gauge and never pauses the consumer. A slow subscription (the case this mode is meant to isolate) makes its queue retain every subsequent message in memory while the main thread keeps fetching. Offset commits cannot advance past that item, so the process holds the entire uncommitted backlog until it OOMs. get_committable_offsets also walks range(start, max_offset+1) under the partition lock, so a large backlog stalls every worker's complete_offset for the duration of that scan.

Shutdown abandons queued work and can block for num_queues * 5s

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run only calls get() while that flag is false. After the current item, the worker exits even if Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) would still return queued items, so those items are never processed and never completed. close() stops and joins the commit thread before joining workers, so items that do finish during shutdown are not committed either. join() ignores its timeout and calls close(). On a deploy/rebalance, in-flight uptime results are redelivered and applied twice (duplicate incidents/occurrences). Joins are also sequential with a 5s timeout each, so 20 workers stuck in slow handlers make close()/terminate() block for about 100s and still drop the work.

An exception in the worker finally kills the only thread for that queue forever

OrderedQueueWorker has no supervisor. complete_offset and metrics.gauge run in the same finally block with no handler, and run() has no outer try around the loop. If gauge (or complete_offset) raises, the thread exits. That queue is the only worker for every group hashed to it, and nothing restarts it. Any offset already queued there stays in outstanding forever, so get_committable_offsets cannot advance that partition. The consumer keeps polling, health checks still pass because poll() only records queue depth, and commits for the partition stop until the process is restarted.

Worker threads never reset Django DB connections, so one DB error drops later results

OrderedQueueWorker calls result_processor on a long-lived thread and never calls django.db.close_old_connections(). Django only runs connection health checks and obsolete-connection cleanup on the request path, which these threads do not have. After an idle timeout, failover, or OperationalError, that thread's connection stays dead. ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows the exception, and the worker's finally still complete_offset, so the failed check is committed and will not be retried. Every later message on that same queue fails the same way and is also acknowledged. One transient DB blip silently disables 1/num_queues of subscription processing until the consumer restarts.

Uptime --mode help still describes the wrong execution model

uptime_options() now accepts thread-queue-parallel, but the help text is still "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." The parallel mode uses a multiprocessing pool, batched-parallel uses a thread pool, and thread-queue-parallel uses one thread per queue. Operators enabling the new flag get no description of what it does or that --max-workers is the queue count rather than a thread-pool size.

The comments claim the ORM handles negative offsets and that this reaches rows outside normal pagination bounds; it does neither, and it does not bypass the organization filter.

A normal non-negative offset behaves as before, but a next cursor with a negative offset used to error and now silently starts at 0, returning the first page instead of the requested window. A previous cursor with a negative offset is still handed to the queryset, and Django raises ValueError, 500ing the request. The new comment says the queryset handles negative offsets; it does not. OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on that field. false_positives.candidate:
Eviction is not atomic with insert and can empty a segment

Span payloads are ZADDed in a separate non-transactional pipeline, and add-buffer.lua never receives the payload or score, so it cannot insert them. The 1000-span cap is a later ZPOPMIN using a count observed inside that script. Redis serializes each script, but two writers can both ZADD past the cap and both compute span_count-1000 from the pre-pop size. ProcessSpansStrategyFactory runs process_batch in a multiprocessing pool when num_processes != 1, and those workers share shards; rebalance/spillover can also double-write a trace. Two scripts that each see 2000 members will each pop 1000 and leave the segment empty. The old set-based union did not delete members on insert, so this data loss is new.

Set-to-sorted-set switch breaks existing span-buffer keys

The buffer keys stay span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id, but the script and SpansBuffer now use ZADD, ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN. The previous code stored those keys as Redis SETs (SADD/SCARD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN). There is no new prefix, TYPE check, or migration. After deploy, every live segment is still a set until redis_ttl (default 3600s). ZADD or ZSCAN on it raises WRONGTYPE, process_spans fails, and the consumer retries the same batch for every in-flight trace. Flush fails the same way, so those segments are neither emitted nor deleted until the key expires.

ZUNIONSTORE SUM and self-union UNLINK drop or mis-rank spans

Merges use ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM. A member present in both inputs (Kafka redelivery, or the same payload written to both the parent key and a child key) gets its end-timestamp scores added, so it sorts as far in the future and ZPOPMIN evicts other spans instead. If the resolved set id equals the current span id, span_key and set_key are the same key: the script unions the key with itself and then UNLINK span_key, deleting the destination the preceding ZADD just wrote. That hits a non-root span whose parent_span_id equals its span_id, or whose redirect chain resolves to its own id. Those spans are gone before flush.

Redirect walk cut from 10000 to 1000 splits deep traces

The parent-redirect loop now stops after 1000 hops, and the comment that this limit fails to join deep segment trees was removed. On a longer chain the loop exits at an intermediate span id, then HSET persists that partial redirect (span_id -> set_span_id). Later spans follow the truncated mapping, so the segment is permanently split and flushed as incomplete pieces. Child-first arrival stores one hop per ancestor, so a trace nested deeper than 1000 spans hits this. The previous cap was 10000 specifically because of that correctness limit.

Hardcoded eviction can drop the root and the flush guard is gone

The cap is ZPOPMIN of span_count-1000 with a literal 1000. SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) is no longer consulted, so that constructor argument does nothing. ZPOPMIN deletes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores with no exception for the segment root, so a root that ended before a child (clock skew or a longer child) is discarded and the flushed segment has no root span. The flush-time check in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, so if insert-time eviction does not run the consumer loads and publishes the whole segment up to the 10MiB byte limit. Evictions are not metered.

No tests for eviction, score order, or the new paginator

Buffer tests were only updated to supply end_timestamp_precise. Every case still uses four or five spans with the same timestamp, so CI never hits ZPOPMIN, never checks that the oldest spans are removed, never checks that the root is kept, and never covers WRONGTYPE on existing set keys or the concurrent double-pop race. The new audit-log OptimizedCursorPaginator path also has no test, so the datetime TypeError and the negative-offset ValueError would not fail CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

Eligibility cache key uses process-randomized hash() and cannot be invalidated

The cache key is error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}. Python hash() is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so workers do not share keys, invalidate_upsampling_cache deletes a different key than other processes wrote, and nothing in this PR calls that invalidator when the allowlist changes anyway. A collision of two project-id tuples in one process also serves the wrong eligibility for 60 seconds and rewrites count() for projects that are not fully allowlisted. Use a stable key (for example a sorted, joined id list) and hook invalidation to allowlist updates, or drop the cache; options.get is already an in-process read.

Both suggest using a deterministic serialization (like a sorted, joined list) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision ignores the dataset and query actually executed

_get_event_stats decides upsampling from the closed-over request dataset and request.GET, not from scoped_dataset or the query argument. Dashboard widget splitting calls this helper with a different dataset and rewritten queries (errors-only "!event.type:transaction", transactions-only "event.type:transaction", and the original metrics dataset). A metrics/discover split therefore either skips upsampling on the errors subquery (outer dataset is not errors/discover) or, when the original request string looks like an error query, applies sum(sample_weight) to the transactions-only probe. Split detection uses those counts (has_errors / has_transactions), so widget discoverSplitDecision can be saved incorrectly, and transaction probes can throw if sample_weight is absent. The eligibility check has to use the dataset and query string passed into this call.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer/request dataset instead of the `scoped_dataset` passed into the helper function, causing upsampling to be skipped during dashboard widget splitting when the original dataset is metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Allowlist option is never registered and is read on every stats query

Every events-stats execution calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, which on a cache miss calls options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", []). This PR never registers that option (no defaults.py or options change). Sentry's options manager raises UnknownOption for unregistered keys even when a default is passed, so a cache miss 500s the whole organization events-stats endpoint, including non-error datasets and projects that should not be upsampled. If a deployment's options.get instead returns the default, the feature never turns on in production; the new tests hide that by mocking options. The lookup also does `project_id in allowlist` with no int/str normalization, so a JSON allowlist of string ids never matches int project ids (feature silently off), and a non-list value raises TypeError on this same hot path.

count() is rewritten to a column string the field parser will not accept

When upsampling is enabled, count() is replaced with the literal "upsampled_count() as count" and passed as a selected column / y-axis. Sentry's field parser treats a column as a function only when the string ends with ')'; this value does not, so it is resolved as a raw column name rather than the new upsampled_count aggregate. Allowlisted error count() stats queries then fail field validation (or, if an alias were accepted, the result key would not stay the `count` field the events-stats contract and the new test expect). Charts, top-events, and any client requesting yAxis=count() for an allowlisted project break instead of returning an upsampled series.

Upsampled count sums sample_weight, but nothing stores the inverse sample rate

upsampled_count is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no ifNull/coalesce. The only write-path change is the test factory, which copies contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate onto sample_rate (the rate itself, e.g. 0.1), not sample_weight, and production ingest is not updated at all. Events therefore have no sample_weight. ClickHouse sum of nulls is 0, so once the rewrite runs, allowlisted error counts become 0 instead of the real count or 1/sample_rate. That also cannot satisfy the new stats test, which stores client_sample_rate 0.1 and expects count == 10. toInt64 additionally truncates any fractional weight. Historical events and transactions that lack the column are zeroed or fail the query rather than falling back to count().

Errors dataset always upsamples, but upsampled_count is only registered on discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True for the errors snuba dataset with no query check, and the endpoint then rewrites count() to upsampled_count(). The new aggregate is added only to the discover dataset function_converter in this PR. Errors timeseries uses its own query builder/config; if that config does not inherit this converter, allowlisted dataset=errors count() requests fail with an unknown function. The new snuba tests never pass dataset=errors (they rely on discover plus event.type:error), so this path is untested and can 400/500 the errors stats API.

Error detection is a substring match and treats negated filters as errors

_is_error_focused_query lowercases the raw query and returns True if it contains the substring "event.type:error". That matches !event.type:error, !(event.type:error), event.type:error OR event.type:transaction, and the token as a prefix of a longer value or inside a message/tag search. For discover queries on allowlisted projects, count() is then rewritten to sum(sample_weight) even when the query is explicitly not errors. Transaction and other non-error events do not have a reliable sample_weight, so those stats queries either error or return zeros/inflated mixed counts. A search parser check for a positive event.type:error condition is required; substring matching is the opposite of the stated caution.

Top-events ranking still uses raw count() while the series is rewritten

For topEvents, only the timeseries y-axis list is passed through transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling. orderby still comes from get_orderby(request) and selected_columns from get_field_list, on both the RPC path (orderby around line 241) and top_events_timeseries (orderby around line 259). A request ordered by count() or -count() therefore ranks the top N groups by the sampled count while the returned series uses upsampled_count. Callers get the wrong groups, or the top-N query fails if it also references the rewritten alias. orderby and any count() in the top-N selected columns need the same transform as the timeseries columns.

Every events-stats query now takes a remote cache round trip

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects always cache.get's before it knows the dataset is errors. That helper runs on every _get_event_stats call, including transaction, span, and metrics queries, and dashboard split runs it several times per request. options.get of the allowlist is already served from the in-process options cache; this adds a shared-cache RTT (and a hard dependency on that cache) on the events-stats hot path to avoid a cheaper lookup. A slow or failing cache delays or fails unrelated stats requests. The allowlist check should happen only after the dataset/query gate, and should not require a remote cache.

Accidental gitlink committed at the PR base commit

This change adds sentry-repo as a gitlink/submodule pointer to a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR base) with no .gitmodules entry and no relation to upsampling. Clones and CI that recurse into submodules, or tools that refuse gitlinks, will fail or nest a second checkout of this repo. The gitlink should be removed before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

Denial entries only dedupe the exact same name and folder, so a sequential sweep of unauthorized resources (list filtering, many GETs) issues one full permission query per resource per 30s instead of the previous single query per user+action. Concurrent checks share one singleflight, but sequential checks do not.

While the golden comment frames the concern around the security risk of trusting stale grants when denials aren't trusted, and the candidate frames it around the performance impact of ignoring cached denials and querying the DB repeatedly, they both fundamentally identify the same underlying design flaw of asymmetric cache trust in the Check operation.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with '_' and no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and parent is often empty, so distinct resources share one key. For example name=foo, parent=bar and name=foo_bar, parent="" both become ..._foo_bar_, and name=abc, parent=de_f matches name=abc_de, parent=f. false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins false denies and skips the DB re-query

That entry is written for every DB deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes it when permissions are granted or the folder cache is refreshed. A check that races ahead of the creator ACL insert (or any deny followed by a grant, including a new wildcard/admin role) therefore stays denied for the full TTL even though the new re-query path would now allow it. On a cold start, N concurrent calls all pass the nil check, queue on the write lock, and each performs a full file read; a later caller whose read fails stores nil and wipes the successful cache published by an earlier caller, so subsequent non-Dev requests miss and can return an error even though a valid asset set was already loaded. Re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock (and do not overwrite a non-nil cache with a failed load). The exclusive lock is also held across the manifest read, so those redundant loads are fully serialized.

Public group members page only loads the first 50 users

setupController always calls Group.findMembers(), and that method now always requests limit 50 (the new model default) and offset 0. The public members template (group/members.hbs) only iterates `members` and has no next/previous controls, unlike the admin group screen. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a non-automatic group and defaulted automatic groups to 200 when no limit was sent. After this change, any group with more than 50 members (including large custom groups and automatic groups such as trust_level_0) silently hides everyone past the first page, with no way to load the rest.

Removing the last member on a page leaves a blank page

findMembers clamps the request offset with Math.min(user_count, offset) using the in-memory user_count, which is only refreshed from the response. removeMember (and addMembers) then call findMembers() without moving offset back. Deleting the last user on the current page therefore re-requests an offset that is now past the end (the clamp still allows offset == old total). The server echoes that offset in meta and returns an empty members array, and the client stores meta.offset, so the admin UI stays on a blank page until Previous is clicked. The members action never clamps offset to the last non-empty page either.

Remove control ignores whether the group is automatic

This row is rendered by the group-member itemView, not in the admin group template's context. Ember's each+itemView sets the row context to the each keyword ({member: user}) or to the user record; neither has the group's automatic flag, and a replaced context does not fall back to the admin-group controller. {{#unless automatic}} is therefore always true, so the remove link is shown for automatic groups (admins, moderators, trust_level_*, and so on). Confirming still calls DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members, which correctly returns 422, but neither the removeMember action nor Group.removeMember handles the failure, so the admin gets a confirm dialog and then no error and no list refresh.

Creating a group drops the chosen alias level

create assigns name and visible, then saves, but never reads params[:alias_level]. The admin form shows the alias-level combo for new groups (it sits outside the {{#if id}} block), and Group.asJSON posts alias_level on create. update does apply alias_level, so editing an existing group works, but the first save always persists the default (0, nobody) no matter what was selected. The client only copies resp.basic_group.id back onto the model, so the UI keeps showing the unsaved choice until the group is reloaded. The new create spec only checks name stripping and would not catch this.

Members limit and offset are unbounded and can 500

The rewritten members action uses limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i and offset = params[:offset].to_i with no upper or lower bound. This route is available to anyone who can see the group, including public automatic groups that contain every user. A very large limit loads and serializes the entire membership in one request. A negative offset or limit is sent through to SQL; PostgreSQL rejects OFFSET/LIMIT < 0, so those query params 500 the endpoint. The old action at least defaulted automatic groups to 200; the rewrite should cap limit (and reject negative offset/limit) rather than trusting the client.

GET /groups/:name/members.json response shape changed

members used to render_serialized an array of GroupUserSerializer objects. It now returns an object {members, meta: {total, limit, offset}}. The in-repo Group.findMembers caller was updated, but this is a public route. Themes, plugins, and API clients that treated the body as an array (for example result.map or a JSON array decode) will break or show no members. There is no compat path, such as keeping the array when limit/offset are omitted, or a versioned response.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match stats are written inside validation and rolled back or double-counted

should_block? is invoked from EmailValidator during User validation, but it is not a pure check: it does match_count += 1, sets last_match_at, and calls save. User#save runs validations inside a transaction and raises ActiveRecord::Rollback when the user is invalid, so the counter update made while rejecting a blocked address is undone and never persisted on a normal save/save!/create. UsersController#create hides this for one path only: it calls user.valid? first (that increment commits) and then user.save (a second increment that rolls back), so the count is right there only by accident and any extra valid? double-counts. The same read-modify-write save also writes every column, so two concurrent matches can lose increments and a concurrent admin change to action_type can be overwritten. Match auditing is unreliable, and the new specs only call should_block? directly so they never catch the rollback.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying issue: the query/check method (`should_block?` / `should_block_email?`) has database-modifying side effects (updating match statistics) during a read/check operation, which leads to race conditions in concurrent environments and unintended behavior when checking validity.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored

email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) after only escaping dots, then uses =~ with no end anchor or domain boundary. A whitelist value of company.com therefore matches user@company.com.attacker.example (and user@company.com.extra) as well as user@company.com, so a site that restricts signup to specific providers can be bypassed by any domain that merely contains the allowed domain as a substring. The same pattern makes a blacklist over-match unrelated hosts such as user@spam.com.legitimate.example. This is now the only server-side domain check (it was moved here from User), and nothing in the new specs covers whitelist or blacklist behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the regex `@(#{domains})` in `email_in_restriction_setting?` lacks proper boundary/end anchoring, allowing attackers to bypass domain whitelists by registering domains that only partially match the allowed domain.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email check is case- and whitespace-sensitive

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact BlockedEmail.where(email: email) match, and BlockedEmail only validates uniqueness of the raw email string (no downcasing or stripping in set_defaults). Signup stores whatever the user typed (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] unchanged), while other paths such as change_email normalize with Email.downcase and strip. A blocked row for "bad@spam.com" therefore does not match "Bad@spam.com" or "bad@spam.com ", and the case-sensitive unique index will not treat those as the same address. Someone who was blocked can still register by changing case or surrounding whitespace.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows blocked users to bypass the check by changing the casing of their email address.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
box-ordinal-group is not shifted to the 1-based scale

@mixin order writes $val unchanged to -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group. Those 2009 properties are 1-based (initial value 1) and reject non-positive integers, while order, -webkit-order, and -ms-flex-order are 0-based (initial value 0). The equivalent legacy value is $val + 1. Today's call sites pass 2 and 3, so they still sort after items that omit order (legacy groups 1, 2, 3 versus modern 0, 2, 3) and the header does not mis-order yet. The shared mixin is still wrong for the model it claims to support: order(1) ties with unstyled siblings instead of following them, and order(0) is an invalid ordinal so the declaration is dropped and the item stays in the default group.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` use a 1-based scale (and reject 0), whereas modern `order` properties are 0-based, so passing `$val` directly without shifting (`$val + 1`) causes bugs when `$val` is 0 or 1.

false_positives.candidate:
Small-action button float is ignored inside the new flex row

.small-action is now a flex container (flexbox() and align-items(center) at lines 264-265), but the action button is still placed with float: right. Float does not apply to flex items, and the patch never replaces it with margin-left: auto on the button or flex: 1 on .small-action-desc. For the usual short small-action label (closed, pinned, archived) in a wide post, the delete button therefore sits immediately after the text instead of at the right edge, which is where float: right put it. The description's old padding (0.5em 0 0.5em 4em) that cleared the 45px floated avatar was also reduced to 0 1.5%, so any browser that ignores every display value emitted by flexbox() still honors float: left on .topic-avatar and draws the label underneath that icon.

Header flex row overflows and pushes controls off-screen

.d-header .contents is now display: flex with the default flex-wrap: nowrap. .title, .extra-info-wrapper (only order: 2 in topic.scss), and .panel (only margin-left: auto and order: 3) never set min-width: 0, overflow: hidden, or flex-shrink: 0. Flex items default to min-width: auto, so they will not shrink below their content minimum, and margin-left: auto only eats positive free space — it does not stop overflow. A wide site logo (this file only sets #site-logo max-height: 40px, not a max-width) or a long docked topic title plus the 32px header icons therefore overflows the bar instead of ellipsizing or wrapping. On a narrow viewport the fixed header widens the page and login/notification controls are pushed out of view. The old float: left / float: right layout kept the panel shrink-to-fit on the right and let the middle content wrap inside the header width. Give the middle item flex: 1, min-width: 0, and overflow: hidden, and set flex-shrink: 0 on .title and .panel.

2009 box display prefixes drop the header float fallback

flexbox() emits display: -webkit-box and display: -moz-box (and inline-flex() emits the inline equivalents) before the 2012 and unprefixed values. Engines that only implement the 2009 box model will honor that display and ignore later ones. That model does not pack with margin-left: auto and ignores float on children, but this PR removed .d-header .title { float: left } and .panel { float: right } and now depends on margin-left: auto to keep login and notification controls on the right. Those browsers therefore lay the logo and the panel out together at the start. Engines that understand none of the prefixed display values also lose the float fallback, so .panel becomes a normal full-width block under the logo. Either omit the 2009 display values and keep the floats as the non-flex fallback, or implement the matching -webkit-box-pack / -webkit-box-flex rules; the prefixes as written do not reproduce the layout they replaced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is never invoked

ActiveModel::Serializer only calls include_<attr>? (every other hook in this file uses that name). include_website_name has no question mark, so it is dead code and the attribute is always serialized. Users with a blank or unparsable website still get website_name: null in /users/:username.json, and any condition placed in this method will not run.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix expected by the Rails serializer (`ActiveModel::Serializer`) for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a minor secondary issue about string concatenation, the core issue is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 website hiding

website is listed in untrusted_attributes, so anonymous viewers of a trust-level 0 user do not receive user_profile.website (anti-spam: the profile must not expose a new user's site). website_name is a new public attribute and is not in that list, and its method reads object.user_profile.website directly. Anonymous clients therefore still get the host, and the path whenever the domain heuristic matches, and user.hbs renders that as the globe label. The new specs never serialize a TL0 user with Guardian.new and assert website_name is absent, so this regression is untested.

Same-domain path display is case-sensitive

website_host is taken from URI#host, which keeps the URL's casing, and is compared to Discourse.current_hostname with == and String#ends_with? (both case-sensitive). A site on example.com and a website of http://Example.com/user, or a site on forums.example.com and a website of http://Example.com/user, fails every branch and the profile shows only the host. The feature then does not show the path for ordinary mixed-case links. The specs only stub lowercase hosts.

Domain check mis-classifies hosts and misses www vs apex

The equal-label branch treats any two hosts with the same label count above 2 as the same site when every label but the first matches. On a forum at mysite.github.io or forum.co.uk, http://evil.github.io/phish and http://other.co.uk/phish are therefore rendered with the full path, not just the host. The else branch (discourse_host.ends_with?("." + website_host)) is true for any dotted suffix, so a website host of com or co.uk is treated as the parent of a normal forum hostname. The check is also asymmetric for the common www case: instance example.com vs website www.example.com/user does not match (label counts differ, and example.com does not end with .www.example.com), so the path is hidden, while instance www.example.com vs website example.com/user does show the path. None of these cases are covered by the new specs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Resize listener accepts any origin that is a prefix of discourseUrl

The check is `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. accept when the sender origin is any substring of discourseUrl, not when it equals the forum origin. A shorter origin that is a prefix matches: if discourseUrl is `https://discuss.example.com`, a window at `https://discuss.example.co` has index 0 and is accepted. That page can postMessage a `discourse-resize` and set the iframe height arbitrarily (hide comments or stretch the frame over the host page). Compare parsed origins for equality, and require index 0 only if a prefix check is kept.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation using `indexOf` is flawed and allows attackers to bypass the check using a forged domain that matches as a substring.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer, so resize is dropped

The embed layout calls `parent.postMessage(..., request.referer)`. postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin (`scheme://host[:port]`), not a full URL with path and query. Browsers drop the message (or throw) when it does not match the parent origin. embed.js also sets the iframe to `scrolling=no` and only grows it on `discourse-resize`, so the comments frame stays at the default height and clips the discussion. Pass the referer origin only (and escape it for the JS string).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `postMessage` is being passed the full referrer URL as the `targetOrigin` instead of just the origin (scheme+host+port), which causes the message to be dropped and breaks iframe resizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
raw_html cook path stores and serves unsanitized HTML

Post#cook returns `raw` unchanged when cook_method is raw_html, skipping PrettyText and Discourse's sanitizer. TopicEmbed.import persists RSS/Readability HTML with that cook method, and the embed view prints it with `raw post.cooked` (the main topic UI also treats cooked as HTML). PollFeed does `CGI.unescapeHTML` on feed content first, so entity-encoded markup becomes live tags, and Readability's allow-list still permits `javascript:`/`data:` href and src. Any feed item or fetched page can therefore plant stored XSS that runs for every forum visitor, not just inside the embed iframe. The imported-from footer makes this worse by interpolating the URL into an href with no escaping (`<a href='#{url}'>` in TopicEmbed.import), so a quote in an otherwise allowed http(s) URL breaks out of the attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues in TopicEmbed.import: a NoMethodError when `contents` is nil, and an XSS vulnerability from unescaped `url` interpolation in the generated HTML (`<a href='#{url}'>`). The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same XSS vulnerability from unescaped URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import (in addition to broader concerns about `raw_html`), though it misses the nil `contents` check. Because it directly hits the specific URL interpolation XSS bug mentioned in the golden comment, it is a match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB (`end if`)

`<%- end if %>` compiles to the Ruby statement `end if`, which is a SyntaxError. Rendering `/embed/best` when a topic already exists (the success path in EmbedController#best) will raise while compiling the template, so the iframe never shows highlights. It must be `<% end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same syntax error in the ERB template where an `if` block is improperly closed with `end if` instead of `end`, which causes a runtime syntax error during rendering.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed poll crashes unless every item has string content

`i.content.scrub` assumes every SimpleRSS item has a String `content`. RSS 2.0 items typically expose `description` and leave `content` nil; Atom can also omit it. Nil (or a non-string) raises NoMethodError, and because there is no rescue the hourly job aborts before later items are imported. `String#scrub` is also Ruby 2.1+ only, so this line fails on Ruby 2.0 even when content is present. Use description/content fallback and guard nil before unescaping.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` will raise a nil exception (NoMethodError) when RSS items lack a `content` field, and it recommends falling back to `description`.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer, so resize is dropped

The embed layout calls `parent.postMessage(..., request.referer)`. postMessage's targetOrigin must be an origin (`scheme://host[:port]`), not a full URL with path and query. Browsers drop the message (or throw) when it does not match the parent origin. embed.js also sets the iframe to `scrolling=no` and only grows it on `discourse-resize`, so the comments frame stays at the default height and clips the discussion. Pass the referer origin only (and escape it for the JS string).
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment focuses on an XSS security vulnerability caused by interpolating an unescaped `request.referer` into JavaScript. While the candidate issue primarily focuses on a functional bug regarding `postMessage` targetOrigin formatting, it explicitly identifies the same code location and notes the need to 'escape it for the JS string' at the end. However, since the primary bug reported by the candidate is functional rather than the XSS vulnerability itself, it is only a partial match, though it catches the required fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Unauthenticated embed URL fetch is an SSRF and topic-spam vector

import_remote uses `open(url).read` (open-uri) with no timeout, size limit, or redirect restriction. EmbedController#best is a public GET whose only gate is `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Referer is client-controlled, so any caller can spoof it and pass `embed_url` on the configured host. TopicRetriever then fetches that URL; open-uri follows redirects to arbitrary hosts (including link-local and cloud metadata). Each miss also enqueues RetrieveTopic with no controller-side dedupe, so unique URLs create unbounded jobs and, on success, topics posted as embed_by_username. open-uri is not even required from this file, so the fetch only works if some other file has already patched Kernel#open.

Embed controller spec expects a sync retrieve the action does not do

The 'no previous embed' example expects `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve` during `get :best`. EmbedController#best only calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`, so mocha fails this example and the job/throttle path is untested. The other success example renders `embed/best`, which currently raises SyntaxError on `end if`, so the `response.should be_success` after-hook fails as well. The spec will not pass as written and does not lock in the async behavior.

Disqus import drops category, original date, and offline permalinks

The importer no longer accepts `--category` and no longer passes `created_at` or `category` into topic creation. It now depends on `TopicEmbed.import_remote`, which HTTP-fetches `t[:link]` and returns nil on any network/HTTP error. The following comment import is skipped entirely when that fetch fails, so a dead or blocked article URL drops the whole Disqus thread instead of creating the previous permalink stub. Category placement and original thread timestamps are also lost, and a single failed fetch aborts the rest of the file because nothing rescues `open`.

embed_url is varchar(255) but used as the unique lookup key

`t.string :embed_url` is a 255-character varchar, with a unique index on that column. TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed and import look up the full URL. Article and RSS links with tracking query strings routinely exceed 255 characters, so insert raises and the topic is never associated; truncated values would also collide or miss on lookup. Store embed_url as text (and index a hash if a unique constraint is still required).

content_sha1 is advanced even when the post is not updated

On change, import always calls `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` after `revise!`, without checking that revise!/save succeeded. PostRevisor#revise! returns false when raw is unchanged and still returns true if `save` fails; either way the SHA is overwritten. The next poll then treats the feed item as already imported and never retries, so the topic body stays stale. If the linked post was deleted, `embed.post` is nil and `PostRevisor.new(post)` raises, which aborts the rest of the feed run. Update the SHA only after a successful save, and skip or recreate when the post is gone.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overwrites the width/height API

Ruby does not overload by arity, so downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) on line 149 replaces downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) on line 145. The width/height wrapper never exists at runtime. Callers that still use the previous signature — numeric max width and max height, which this pull request does not update anywhere else — now bind the height integer to opts. optimize then evaluates opts[:allow_animation] and raises NoMethodError instead of building a widthxheight geometry, so those calls 500.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice in Ruby, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to overwrite the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), which breaks callers using the separate width/height signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client size check hardcoded to 10MB for every type

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments each honored their admin setting. It now always uses 10 * 1024. Attachments larger than 10MB are rejected even when max_attachment_size_kb allows them, and attachments between the real attachment limit and 10MB pass the client and fail only on the server. Images are capped at 10MB regardless of max_image_size_kb, so a site that allows larger images cannot upload them from the browser. The 413 handler on line 246 uses the same hardcode, so the dialog always claims the limit is 10240 KB even when the web server or site setting differs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: hardcoding `10 * 1024` instead of using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` for both the upload validation and the 413 error handler, causing client-side limits to diverge from server-side and per-type settings.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
80% geometry breaks animation and does not enforce the size limit

The new call passes "80%" and allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When that setting is false, downsize_instructions runs convert with a [0] frame selector, so a large animated GIF or multi-page image is permanently flattened to the first frame in the stored original; that setting is about thumbnails, not the upload. When it is true, gifsicle --resize-fit is given "80%", but it requires a pixel size such as 100x100, so it exits non-zero. The failure is ignored, and after five attempts the still-oversized file is passed to Upload.create_for anyway. The loop also does not fail the upload if the file is still larger than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb after five 80% passes, so the comment's "reduced to allowed size" guarantee is not enforced for JPEGs or PNGs either.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: passing '80%' to `gifsicle --resize-fit` when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is true fails because gifsicle expects pixel dimensions (e.g., 100x100) rather than a percentage, and the failure is ignored.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize reads and writes the same tempfile

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both source and destination. convert (and gifsicle when animation is enabled) opens the output for writing before the input is fully read, and ImageMagick truncates that path immediately. This tempfile is the only copy of the upload, so a large image can become empty or partial before Upload.create_for. The loop also ignores downsize's false return, so a failed conversion is retried against the already truncated file and then handed to create_for. Write to a separate tempfile and replace the original only after a successful non-empty result.

API URL downloads capped at a hardcoded 10MB for all types

FileHelper.download's limit changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to 10.megabytes for every upload type, not only images that will be downsized. Non-image API URL uploads are therefore cut off at 10MB even when max_attachment_size_kb is higher, and they are no longer tied to the attachment setting at all. Image URL uploads also cannot exceed 10MB when max_image_size_kb is configured above that, so the admin setting and the new downscale path disagree.

No input size ceiling before repeated ImageMagick runs

The browser and the URL-download path are capped at 10MB, but the multipart file branch never checks an upper bound before the downsize loop. true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

The new working-hours test uses Array.find and returns unavailable if the slot falls outside any single window whose days include the slot's UTC weekday. A host with a lunch break, or a single local range that getWorkingHours splits across UTC midnight into two entries on the same day, therefore fails the check for every slot: a 10:00 slot inside 09:00–12:00 is still outside 13:00–17:00, so find matches and the slot is dropped. The booking page then shows no times. The condition is also inverted for days off: if no window lists that weekday, find matches nothing and the host is treated as free, so a fixed host who does not work that day is not actually blocked. The same find() treats "outside this one override" as a hard unavailable: two override windows on the same day reject a slot that sits in only one of them, because the other window's callback returns true. Zero-length overrides (the unavailable-day convention, start equal to end) are detected with dayjs object ===, which is never true for two instances, so that branch never runs. Day matching compares dayjs(date.start).add(offset).format (process-local mode) to slotStartTime.format (UTC mode), so when the server TZ is not UTC the override is attached to the wrong calendar day or ignored. When the wrapped end is less than the wrapped start, buildSlots drops the range (start >= end), so the override disappears. true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount write is not atomic under overlapping crons

Both failure paths set retryCount to the in-memory reminder.retryCount + 1 (here and in the catch at line 195) instead of an atomic increment. The handler loops every due reminder with several queries and a Twilio call, and it is a cron POST that can be invoked again if the previous run is still going or the scheduler retries a timeout. Two runs read the same count, both can call scheduleSMS for the same unscheduled row, and both write the same retryCount, so the retryCount > 1 delete never observes the real number of attempts and does not stop duplicate sends. Use retryCount: { increment: 1 } and claim the row before calling Twilio so a second run cannot schedule it again.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: updating `retryCount` using `reminder.retryCount + 1` in both the normal failure path and the catch block is not atomic and leads to lost increments under concurrent execution. true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
