The next cron then deletes those rows. Email and WhatsApp reminders are dropped and never send. A scheduled SMS loses its referenceId without cancelling the provider message, so the text can still go out and can no longer be tracked or cancelled. The original delete was limited to SMS; that limit was not applied to this OR branch. Scope it to unscheduled SMS rows this job actually failed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the deleteMany OR branch with retryCount > 1 lacks the SMS method filter, causing it to inadvertently delete Email and WhatsApp workflow reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Broad catch burns the two-strike limit and can duplicate SMS

The catch surrounds template building, the organizer profile lookup, getBookerBaseUrl, twilio.scheduleSMS, and the success update that sets scheduled and referenceId. Any throw increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false. If Twilio already accepted the message and only the following update failed, the SID is discarded and the next cron calls scheduleSMS again, sending a duplicate; after two such errors retryCount is 2 and the opening deleteMany removes the row while those provider messages stay queued. The same path treats transient failures (DB blip, booker URL, empty attendees) as permanent send failures. This cron loads every unscheduled SMS in the next 7 days, so two errored passes delete that whole backlog and those bookings never get an SMS. Only count a retry when the provider rejects the send, and if scheduleSMS already returned a SID, persist that SID instead of incrementing.

Missing number or empty body is retried until the send date

retryCount is incremented only when message is non-empty and sendTo is set, and only if scheduleSMS returns a falsy value or throws. If the step has no sendTo, the booking has no smsReminderNumber, or the rendered body is empty, the loop just continues. The row stays scheduled false with retryCount 0 and is selected again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop (invalid or missing phone). Treat a missing destination or empty message as a terminal failure so those reminders are not loaded until the event date.

retryCount delete is not covered by an index

deleteMany now ORs retryCount > 1 onto the cleanup, but WorkflowReminder only indexes (method, scheduled, scheduledDate), (bookingUid), (workflowStepId), (seatReferenceId), and (cancelled, scheduledDate). The new column in schema.prisma has no index. Postgres cannot serve that OR branch from the existing composite index, so every cron run can sequentially scan WorkflowReminder before any SMS is scheduled. That table grows with bookings; a slow cleanup makes this endpoint more likely to overlap the next cron tick.

This change deletes reminder rows and stops SMS after a small number of failures, and nothing in the PR covers that contract. Needed cases: one failure leaves the row and a second failure makes the next run delete it; the gt: 1 cutoff matches "failed twice" and does not allow a third scheduleSMS call; EMAIL and WHATSAPP rows with any retryCount are not deleted; a falsy scheduleSMS result and a thrown provider error both increment; empty sendTo or an empty body does not get reselected until the date; a successful schedule does not increment and is not deleted while still in the future. Without those, the unscoped OR and the two-strike catch can drop or duplicate reminders unnoticed.

The comment says this deletes scheduled SMS reminders whose scheduled date is already past. The query never filters on scheduled true, and the new OR branch also deletes any method's reminder with retryCount > 1, including future rows. Someone editing this later from the comment can restore or narrow the wrong predicate and either resurrect the infinite retry or keep deleting email and WhatsApp reminders.

Team/org auth SQL is an ungrouped OR, so extra AND filters skip team bookings

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition return a top-level OR, e.g. (("teamId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)), with no parentheses around the whole predicate. getBaseConditions returns that fragment unchanged whenever there is no eventTypeId/memberUserId filter (the common path; date bounds are not part of InsightsBookingServiceFilterOptions and must be applied by the caller). AND binds tighter than OR, so WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ${start} AND "startTime" < ${end} is parsed as (team-booking match) OR (personal-booking match AND date range). Every team booking for that team/org is returned with no time bound, and any other caller AND (event-type allow-list, status, extra auth) is likewise dropped for the team-booking side. The same trap exists on the public event-type filter at the ungrouped OR in buildFilterConditions ("eventTypeId" = $1 OR "eventParentId" = $1): WHERE auth AND that fragment becomes (auth AND eventTypeId = $1) OR eventParentId = $1, which can return rows outside authorization. getBaseConditions only parenthesizes when both auth and filters are present, and the tests assert the ungrouped form, so they do not catch this. Wrap every returned fragment in an outer (...) so it is one grouped predicate before it is embedded.

ANY(${number[]}) does not bind a Postgres array, so team/org auth queries fail

Org and team authorization interpolate JavaScript number arrays as Prisma.sql`"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds})` (same pattern at the team-scope user list). Prisma.sql binds each interpolated value as one query parameter; a JS array is not expanded into a PostgreSQL int[]. At execution this typically errors with operator does not exist: integer = text or malformed array literal (the parameter is sent as text/JSON like [1,2,3], not '{1,2,3}'::int[]). Team and org insights then throw instead of returning rows. The length > 0 guard avoids an empty list but does not fix binding. Use a form Prisma actually supports, such as "teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)}) or "teamId" = ANY(ARRAY[${Prisma.join(teamIds)}]::int[]), and keep the empty-list guard because Prisma.join([]) produces invalid IN (). The new tests never execute these statements: they deep-compare Sql objects, and the only $queryRaw case is user scope, which has no ANY().

Composed-condition assertions compare nested Sql objects to flat templates

Team scope (this expect), org scope, and the combined eventTypeId+memberUserId filter expect a single flat Prisma.sql`...` template. The service builds those predicates with reduce, nesting fragments (Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` / AND). Prisma stores nested Sql instances on .values and only flattens them when the query runs, so Vitest toEqual compares different .strings/.values and these tests fail even if the rendered SQL matches. The author noted the suite was not run. User-scope and single-filter expects happen to be one template on both sides and can pass while the composed authorization paths stay red and unexecuted. Assert rendered SQL (or execute team/org conditions with $queryRaw, including a row that must be excluded) instead of structural equality of differently built Sql objects.

When externalCalendarId is null or omitted, the find compares every calendar to that same falsy value and never matches, so selectedCalendar/calendarId is undefined. Previously this fell back to destinationCalendar.externalId. updateEvent then calls Google with calendarId undefined and the reschedule/update fails; deleteEvent falls through to "primary" and leaves the event on a non-primary calendar. CalendarManager.deleteEvent still calls deleteEvent(uid, event) without an external id, and any booking reference with a null externalCalendarId hits this path. true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateAllCalendarEvents calls updateEvent with a missing credential

When a calendar reference has a credentialId that is not on the EventManager user, the code loads it from the DB, but if that lookup misses (deleted credential, or app.slug absent so the rebuild is skipped) it still pushes updateEvent(credential, ...) with credential undefined. getCalendar then throws on credential.type. That rejection fails Promise.all for every calendar reference in the batch, and the catch returns synthetic failures and no longer console.errors the message it builds, so a reschedule/location update can report total failure after partially applying. createAllCalendarEvents correctly skips a missing credential; this path does not.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: in `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when `reference.credentialId` is present on a reference, the `credential` lookup can fail and leave `credential` as `undefined`, yet it is still passed into `updateEvent(credential, ...)`, causing a runtime error.

false_positives.candidate:
Video booking references no longer store credentialId

In create(), referencesToCreate now sets credentialId only for calendar results (`isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`). Video results previously kept result.credentialId. handleCancelBooking deletes the meeting only when bookingVideoReference.credentialId is set and looks that credential up; with credentialId always omitted, cancelling a new booking never calls deleteMeeting, so Zoom/Daily/Meet links stay live after cancel. updateLocation() still copies result.credentialId, so only the initial create path is broken.

Collective co-host calendars dropped when organizer has none

evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when both eventType.destinationCalendar and organizerUser.destinationCalendar are missing, and the collective branch then does evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars). Optional push on null is a no-op, so every co-host destination calendar collected above is discarded. createAllCalendarEvents then takes the empty/null path and its fallback filters credentials with type === "calendar", which never matches google_calendar/office365_calendar/etc. A collective booking whose first host has no destination calendar creates no host calendar events at all, which is the case this PR is meant to fix.

Only the first destination calendar is stored on the booking

The booking create connects only evt.destinationCalendar[0]. Booking.destinationCalendar is a single relation, and confirm.handler, the Stripe and PayPal payment webhooks, edit location, and the booking reminder all rebuild CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar from that one row (or the organizer user row) wrapped in an array. Those paths call EventManager.create/update. Collective bookings that defer calendar creation until confirmation or payment therefore never see co-host destination calendars, so only the organizer gets a calendar event. The in-memory array built for the initial request is not recoverable later.

Cancelling remaining recurring bookings does not delete each host calendar event

The new per-reference loop wraps the recurring allRemainingBookings branch unchanged. For every calendar reference that has a credentialId, that branch ignores the reference just fetched and instead walks every organizer calendar credential and, for each remaining instance, references.find() of the first _calendar ref only, then deleteEvent on that uid. Co-host references are never selected, so their recurring events stay on the calendar. The same first event is deleted once per outer reference times every organizer calendar credential, and the credential loaded for the current reference is unused. Non-recurring cancel correctly deletes each reference with its own credential; recurring cancel does not.

Seat-merge reschedule deletes only one old calendar event

When newBookingId is set, updateAllCalendarEvents still does booking.references.find() for a single _calendar reference and deletes only that uid. Collective bookings now store one calendar reference per host. Merging a seated booking onto an existing slot therefore removes one host's old event and leaves the other hosts' events at the old time.

Request-reschedule does not delete co-host calendar events

Calendar cleanup builds credentialsMap from getUsersCredentials(user.id) keyed only by credential.type, then deleteEvent uses credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type). Collective bookings now have one calendar reference per host, often the same type (google_calendar) but different credentialIds. The map keeps a single credential for that type, and co-host credential ids on the references are ignored, so co-host events are deleted with the requesting user's token (Google 404) and remain on the co-host calendar. handleCancelBooking was updated to load credentialId from the DB; this path was not.

Webhook destinationCalendar shape is a breaking, inconsistent change

CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar changed from a single DestinationCalendar | null to an array, and that object is spread into BOOKING_CREATED / BOOKING_CANCELLED / BOOKING_REJECTED webhook payloads. Consumers reading payload.destinationCalendar.externalId or .integration will break; the PR is marked non-breaking and does not version the payload. Emitters also disagree on the empty value: handleNewBooking still assigns null, while confirm, cancel, payment webhooks, and the rejected webhook e2e expectation use []. BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests still expect null, so clients cannot rely on one empty shape either.

Last calendar result overwrites evt.iCalUID

While building references, every calendar result assigns evt.iCalUID = result.iCalUID. createAllCalendarEvents now returns one result per host calendar, and each Google insert has its own iCalUID. The assignment keeps only the last host's UID on the shared event object that callers use for confirmation emails and ICS. Attendee clients can then fail to match the organizer's event. The UID is also not fed into later createEvent calls, so the host events are not correlated with each other either.

No test covers multi-host destination calendars

The PR checklist says no tests were added. Nothing covers createAllCalendarEvents with two destination calendars, the Google Meet empty-array crash, co-host calendars when the organizer destination is null, video reference credentialId, recurring cancel of multiple calendar references, or the webhook payload shape. The only e2e edit changes BOOKING_REJECTED destinationCalendar from null to [] and would not catch these regressions.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule returns before calendar and video cleanup

requestReschedule now uses bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) so it can await getCalendar, but forEach does not wait for those promises. The mutation marks the booking CANCELLED, sends the reschedule email, fires BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and resolves while calendar.deleteEvent and deleteMeeting may not have started. Previously getCalendar was synchronous, so deleteEvent was at least invoked before the handler continued. Now the first await yields before any provider call, and a serverless isolate can exit before the dynamic import finishes. Rejected imports or delete failures are unhandled rejections with no surrounding try/catch. Collect the work with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) and await both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting before sending email or returning.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment focuses specifically on adding a try-catch around an await to handle dynamic import failures gracefully. While the candidate issue primarily focuses on the async/await anti-pattern inside a `forEach` loop causing premature return, it also explicitly points out the exact issue from the golden comment: 'Rejected imports or delete failures are unhandled rejections with no surrounding try/catch.'

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Vital reschedule does not wait for calendar or video deletion

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) does not await its callbacks, and the try/catch around it cannot see rejections from them. getCalendar is now async, so calendar.deleteEvent is not even started until that import resolves, and neither deleteEvent nor deleteMeeting is awaited. Reschedule then sends the reschedule email and returns true while the external calendar event and video meeting may still exist. On serverless, the handler can be frozen after the response, so the cleanup often never runs and the old slot stays busy. Failures become unhandled promise rejections. Replace this with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) and await both deleteEvent and deleteMeeting inside the mapper.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: using `forEach` with `async` callbacks for calendar and video event deletions, which causes promises to not be awaited, bypasses surrounding try-catch blocks, and leads to unhandled promise rejections and incomplete cleanup. Both suggest replacing `forEach` with `Promise.all` and `map`.

false_positives.candidate:
WipeMyCal reschedule does not wait for calendar or video deletion

The same forEach(async) pattern was introduced here when getCalendar became async. Array.forEach ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, so the try/catch never observes getCalendar, deleteEvent, or deleteMeeting failures, and the function sends the reschedule email and returns true without waiting for those calls. Because the first await is now the dynamic app import, deletion is no longer even initiated before the handler continues. Serverless runtimes can freeze after the response and drop that work, leaving the cancelled event on the user's calendar and the slot blocked. Await Promise.all over a map, and await deleteEvent and deleteMeeting inside it.

Recurring cancel races calendar deletion against Promise.all

When cancelling all remaining instances of a recurring event, credentials are still walked with forEach(async), and this change added await getCalendar inside that callback before deleteEvent. forEach does not wait, and apiDeletes.push only happens after both awaits, so the later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) (around line 652) usually runs while apiDeletes still lacks these deletions — often before deleteEvent has been called at all. The non-recurring else branch just below was correctly rewritten to a for-loop that awaits getCalendar and pushes the delete promise before continuing; the recurring branch was not. The handler can therefore return success while series events remain on the external calendar and those times stay busy. Errors in the callback are unhandled rejections. Await Promise.all on the credential list (and on each deleteEvent) instead of forEach, and push the promises before awaiting them if they must be included in apiDeletes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard metric tags break tag parsing

shard_tag is a comma-joined list of every shard a process owns and is emitted as a metric tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce (key shard) and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce (key shards). DogStatsD, which sentry.utils.metrics uses, treats commas as tag separators, so a value like 0,1,2 is parsed as extra tags and the series is dropped or attributed to the wrong tags. With the new CLI default --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so this is the default path whenever a consumer has more than one partition. The value is also unique per partition assignment, so rebalances create a high-cardinality series. wait_produce uses the key shards while produce uses shard, so the two timers cannot be correlated. Emit a bounded process index, or one tag per shard, and use the same key.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate emphasizes comma-separated tag values, it also explicitly identifies the inconsistent 'shard' versus 'shards' keys on produce and wait_produce metrics and explains that this prevents correlation. That matches the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without force-stopping flusher processes

SpanFlusher.join sets stopped and then calls next_step.join with the full timeout. If that consumes the budget, remaining_time <= 0 and the loop breaks without process.terminate() for every flusher process. close() intentionally does not stop these processes (to avoid a Redis memory spike at the start of rebalance), so join is the only force-stop path. Arroyo calls join with a finite timeout on shutdown and rebalance, and the consumer process stays alive across rebalance, so an un-killed flusher keeps flushing shards this consumer no longer owns. Those segments race the new assignee and are produced again to the buffered-segments topic. The wait is also sequential, so one slow process can exhaust the deadline and skip terminate() for the rest. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. After signaling stop, join must terminate and reap every process even when the timeout is already spent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same shutdown bug: when the timeout budget is exhausted, breaking out of the loop skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running. The candidate adds context and consequences but matches the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart overlaps two flushers on the same shards

_ensure_processes_alive SIGKILLs a hung flusher and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards without joining the old process. Process.kill() only sends the signal and returns, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, Kafka produce, or done_flush_segments while the replacement starts flushing the same shard list. Both then read and clear the same Redis segments and emit them to buffered-segments, duplicating downstream data, and they also race on the shared backpressure_since and healthy_since values. The old Process object is dropped without being reaped, so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits. The replacement must be started only after the previous process has actually exited.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error context is paired by dict value order, not node id

fetch_error_details loads nodestore blobs with get_multi(node_ids) and then zips error_ids with events.values(). get_multi returns a dict keyed by node id; value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, and backends that omit missing keys shift every subsequent pair. The summary sent to Seer can attribute the wrong title, message, and timestamp to an error id, or drop the wrong events via the data is not None filter. Lookups need to be events.get(node_id) for each id. Timestamps are also used raw in gen_request_data comparisons; a non-numeric nodestore timestamp (ISO string) raises TypeError and fails the whole summarize request.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: zipping error_ids with events.values() assumes matching order, which can associate event data with the wrong ID when dictionary ordering differs or missing keys shift alignment. The additional timestamp concern does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

Reporting API age of 0 (report just generated) and timestamp of 0 are valid integers allowed by the field constraints, but both are falsy, so a report that includes both is accepted. Neither field is required, so a report with neither age nor timestamp also passes even though each spec needs one of them.

Its additional concern about neither field being supplied does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Suspect-issue PR comments call methods that do not exist on the workflow

get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, but _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration, not on PRCommentWorkflow. PRCommentWorkflow is a separate workflow type that holds an integration; it does not gain that staticmethod. GitHubPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow.get_comment_body also call self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template and self.get_environment_info, which were added only on CommitContextIntegration. Generating a merged-PR suspect-issue comment therefore raises AttributeError and the GitHub/GitLab comment workflow fails instead of posting.

Issue titles are interpolated into markdown links unsanitized

MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE places the issue title inside a markdown link label: [**{title}**]({url}). Issue titles are attacker-controlled error text and are only length-truncated, not escaped. A title containing ](https://evil.example) or a newline closes the link early and can inject extra markdown into the comment the Sentry bot posts on the customer's GitHub/GitLab PR. Environment names are likewise dropped into the comment in backticks with no escaping.

Replay error lookup depends on date filters the client never sends

Every summarize request now calls get_filter_params and query_replay_instance before building logs, and process_raw_response is given request.query_params.getlist('field'). The replay AI tab requests /summarize/breadcrumbs/ with no start, end, statsPeriod, or field=error_ids. If get_filter_params rejects a missing range, the previously working summary 400s. If it defaults to a recent window, error_ids is empty for replays outside that window, so error context is silently omitted. A Snuba failure also 500s a path that previously only needed recording segments. error_ids must be requested explicitly and the replay's own time range used, not the caller's page filters.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the search filter branch. When searchQuery is empty the function returns sortAttributes(attributes) immediately, so those internal fields stay visible in the default attributes tree. They disappear only after the user types a query, including when the query would otherwise match them. The exclusion needs to run before the early return.

Feedback summary ignores environment (and search) page filters

useFeedbackSummary requests /feedback-summary/ with only the normalized datetime and selection.projects. The feedback list page is scoped by the page-filter environment selection (and the search box), but those are not sent. With an environment selected, the Seer summary describes all environments in the projects while the list shows one environment, so the summary does not match the data on screen.

Feedback list no longer fills the grid cell and will not scroll

The list grid area used to be a FluidHeight Container, which constrained height and scrolled the list inside the 1fr row. It is now SummaryListContainer, a flex column with no min-height: 0, overflow: hidden, or height: 100%. Grid items default to min-height: auto, so the column grows with the summary plus the full list instead of staying in the viewport row, and the inner FluidHeight percentage height does not resolve to the leftover space. The feedback list scroll pane breaks once the summary is shown.

Attribute key hook returns undefined after a failed fetch

The old hook always reduced the response into a TagCollection, so a failed request still yielded {}. The new hook returns useQuery data directly (attributes: isFetching ? previous : data) and dropped retry: false. On error, data is undefined and isFetching is false, so attributes becomes undefined. Explore callers that spread or index attributes (string tags, number tags, has-tag) will throw when the trace-item attributes endpoint fails. Default react-query retry (3) and refetchOnWindowFocus also replace the previous retry: false and refetchOnWindowFocus: false, multiplying load on that endpoint.

60s deadline is too short for a 100-identity SSO refresh batch

check_auth_identities now has processing_deadline_duration=60 while check_auth still hands it up to chunk_size (100) identities. Each identity can do an external IdP refresh. check_auth stamps last_synced before enqueueing this task, so if the worker kills the task at 60s the remaining identities are not refreshed and will not be selected again until the next AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL (about a day). SSO validity checks are skipped for the tail of every oversized batch.

AI summary treats an unloaded project as missing

Project is resolved with useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id}), which is undefined both while the project list is still loading and when the project truly does not exist. The new branch returns 'Project not found' whenever project_id is set and project is missing, before the isPending check, and the summarize query stays disabled. Users hit a hard error (at least a flash, or a stuck error if projects never include that id yet) instead of waiting for the project store.

Concurrent first searches, watch events, or init workers for the same NamespacedResource therefore build two bleve indexes. The later cache write blindly overwrites the earlier one, so one caller keeps writing and searching an index that is no longer in the cache while everyone else uses the other. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any BuildIndex error aborts server construction, so the next start hits the same bleve.New error and the process cannot boot until the directory is deleted by hand. One worker can return another worker's nil and hide a failed namespace build, so startup continues after an index failed (the opposite of the comment that any init failure must block startup), or a success can be overwritten and fail startup incorrectly. The span attribute namespaced_indexed is also racy. This function is now on the blocking startup path.

Arroyo closes the strategy and calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory on every partition revoke/assign, so the next strategy is handed a pool whose queues reject puts and whose workers are dead. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit then hits the bare except, logs, and add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The commit thread treats that as success and commits offset+1. After the first rebalance or consumer restart-in-process, every uptime result is acknowledged and dropped. The consumer thread is simultaneously in poll()/submit(). confluent-kafka Consumer objects are not thread-safe, and Arroyo's commit policy mutates shared offset state that is only used from the processing thread elsewhere. Concurrent commit and poll can crash the consumer, skip commits, or publish a torn offset map. terminate() only sets shutdown_event and does not join this thread, so it can still be inside commit_function after the processor has closed the consumer. close() joins the thread for at most 5s and then continues, so a slow commit leaves two commit threads if a new strategy is created. Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit() always put()s without blocking. The class docstring says queues provide natural backpressure, but poll() only emits a gauge and never pauses the consumer. A slow subscription (the case this mode is meant to isolate) makes its queue retain every subsequent message in memory while the main thread keeps fetching. Offset commits cannot advance past that item, so the process holds the entire uncommitted backlog until it OOMs. get_committable_offsets also walks range(start, max_offset+1) under the partition lock, so a large backlog stalls every worker's complete_offset for the duration of that scan.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, and OrderedQueueWorker.run only calls get() while that flag is false. After the current item, the worker exits even if Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) would still return queued items, so those items are never processed and never completed. close() stops and joins the commit thread before joining workers, so items that do finish during shutdown are not committed either. join() ignores its timeout and calls close(). On a deploy/rebalance, in-flight uptime results are redelivered and applied twice (duplicate incidents/occurrences). Joins are also sequential with a 5s timeout each, so 20 workers stuck in slow handlers make close()/terminate() block for about 100s and still drop the work.

An exception in the worker finally kills the only thread for that queue forever

OrderedQueueWorker has no supervisor. complete_offset and metrics.gauge run in the same finally block with no handler, and run() has no outer try around the loop. If gauge (or complete_offset) raises, the thread exits. That queue is the only worker for every group hashed to it, and nothing restarts it. Any offset already queued there stays in outstanding forever, so get_committable_offsets cannot advance that partition. The consumer keeps polling, health checks still pass because poll() only records queue depth, and commits for the partition stop until the process is restarted.

Worker threads never reset Django DB connections, so one DB error drops later results

OrderedQueueWorker calls result_processor on a long-lived thread and never calls django.db.close_old_connections(). Django only runs connection health checks and obsolete-connection cleanup on the request path, which these threads do not have. After an idle timeout, failover, or OperationalError, that thread's connection stays dead. ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows the exception, and the worker's finally still complete_offset, so the failed check is committed and will not be retried. Every later message on that same queue fails the same way and is also acknowledged. One transient DB blip silently disables 1/num_queues of subscription processing until the consumer restarts.

Uptime --mode help still describes the wrong execution model

uptime_options() now accepts thread-queue-parallel, but the help text is still "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." The parallel mode uses a multiprocessing pool, batched-parallel uses a thread pool, and thread-queue-parallel uses one thread per queue. Operators enabling the new flag get no description of what it does or that --max-workers is the queue count rather than a thread-pool size.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction is not atomic with insert and can empty a segment

Span payloads are ZADDed in a separate non-transactional pipeline, and add-buffer.lua never receives the payload or score, so it cannot insert them. The 1000-span cap is a later ZPOPMIN using a count observed inside that script. Redis serializes each script, but two writers can both ZADD past the cap and both compute span_count-1000 from the pre-pop size. ProcessSpansStrategyFactory runs process_batch in a multiprocessing pool when num_processes != 1, and those workers share shards; rebalance/spillover can also double-write a trace. Two scripts that each see 2000 members will each pop 1000 and leave the segment empty. The old set-based union did not delete members on insert, so this data loss is new.

Set-to-sorted-set switch breaks existing span-buffer keys

The buffer keys stay span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id, but the script and SpansBuffer now use ZADD, ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN. The previous code stored those keys as Redis SETs (SADD/SCARD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN). There is no new prefix, TYPE check, or migration. After deploy, every live segment is still a set until redis_ttl (default 3600s). ZADD or ZSCAN on it raises WRONGTYPE, process_spans fails, and the consumer retries the same batch for every in-flight trace. Flush fails the same way, so those segments are neither emitted nor deleted until the key expires.

ZUNIONSTORE SUM and self-union UNLINK drop or mis-rank spans

Merges use ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM. A member present in both inputs (Kafka redelivery, or the same payload written to both the parent key and a child key) gets its end-timestamp scores added, so it sorts as far in the future and ZPOPMIN evicts other spans instead. If the resolved set id equals the current span id, span_key and set_key are the same key: the script unions the key with itself and then UNLINK span_key, deleting the destination the preceding ZADD just wrote. That hits a non-root span whose parent_span_id equals its span_id, or whose redirect chain resolves to its own id. Those spans are gone before flush.

Redirect walk cut from 10000 to 1000 splits deep traces

The parent-redirect loop now stops after 1000 hops, and the comment that this limit fails to join deep segment trees was removed. On a longer chain the loop exits at an intermediate span id, then HSET persists that partial redirect (span_id -> set_span_id). Later spans follow the truncated mapping, so the segment is permanently split and flushed as incomplete pieces. Child-first arrival stores one hop per ancestor, so a trace nested deeper than 1000 spans hits this. The previous cap was 10000 specifically because of that correctness limit.

Hardcoded eviction can drop the root and the flush guard is gone

The cap is ZPOPMIN of span_count-1000 with a literal 1000. SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) is no longer consulted, so that constructor argument does nothing. ZPOPMIN deletes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores with no exception for the segment root, so a root that ended before a child (clock skew or a longer child) is discarded and the flushed segment has no root span. The flush-time check in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, so if insert-time eviction does not run the consumer loads and publishes the whole segment up to the 10MiB byte limit. Evictions are not metered.

No tests for eviction, score order, or the new paginator

Buffer tests were only updated to supply end_timestamp_precise. Every case still uses four or five spans with the same timestamp, so CI never hits ZPOPMIN, never checks that the oldest spans are removed, never checks that the root is kept, and never covers WRONGTYPE on existing set keys or the concurrent double-pop race. The new audit-log OptimizedCursorPaginator path also has no test, so the datetime TypeError and the negative-offset ValueError would not fail CI.

The eligibility check has to use the dataset and query string passed into this call.

Its additional query-related claims do not negate this match.

Allowlist option is never registered and is read on every stats query

Every events-stats execution calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, which on a cache miss calls options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", []). This PR never registers that option (no defaults.py or options change). Sentry's options manager raises UnknownOption for unregistered keys even when a default is passed, so a cache miss 500s the whole organization events-stats endpoint, including non-error datasets and projects that should not be upsampled. If a deployment's options.get instead returns the default, the feature never turns on in production; the new tests hide that by mocking options. The lookup also does `project_id in allowlist` with no int/str normalization, so a JSON allowlist of string ids never matches int project ids (feature silently off), and a non-list value raises TypeError on this same hot path.

When upsampling is enabled, count() is replaced with the literal "upsampled_count() as count" and passed as a selected column / y-axis. Sentry's field parser treats a column as a function only when the string ends with ')'; this value does not, so it is resolved as a raw column name rather than the new upsampled_count aggregate. Allowlisted error count() stats queries then fail field validation (or, if an alias were accepted, the result key would not stay the `count` field the events-stats contract and the new test expect). Charts, top-events, and any client requesting yAxis=count() for an allowlisted project break instead of returning an upsampled series.

Upsampled count sums sample_weight, but nothing stores the inverse sample rate

upsampled_count is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no ifNull/coalesce. The only write-path change is the test factory, which copies contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate onto sample_rate (the rate itself, e.g. 0.1), not sample_weight, and production ingest is not updated at all. Events therefore have no sample_weight. ClickHouse sum of nulls is 0, so once the rewrite runs, allowlisted error counts become 0 instead of the real count or 1/sample_rate. That also cannot satisfy the new stats test, which stores client_sample_rate 0.1 and expects count == 10. toInt64 additionally truncates any fractional weight. Historical events and transactions that lack the column are zeroed or fail the query rather than falling back to count().

Errors dataset always upsamples, but upsampled_count is only registered on discover

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True for the errors snuba dataset with no query check, and the endpoint then rewrites count() to upsampled_count(). The new aggregate is added only to the discover dataset function_converter in this PR. Errors timeseries uses its own query builder/config; if that config does not inherit this converter, allowlisted dataset=errors count() requests fail with an unknown function. The new snuba tests never pass dataset=errors (they rely on discover plus event.type:error), so this path is untested and can 400/500 the errors stats API.

Error detection is a substring match and treats negated filters as errors

_is_error_focused_query lowercases the raw query and returns True if it contains the substring "event.type:error". That matches !event.type:error, !(event.type:error), event.type:error OR event.type:transaction, and the token as a prefix of a longer value or inside a message/tag search. For discover queries on allowlisted projects, count() is then rewritten to sum(sample_weight) even when the query is explicitly not errors. Transaction and other non-error events do not have a reliable sample_weight, so those stats queries either error or return zeros/inflated mixed counts. A search parser check for a positive event.type:error condition is required; substring matching is the opposite of the stated caution.

Top-events ranking still uses raw count() while the series is rewritten

For topEvents, only the timeseries y-axis list is passed through transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling. orderby still comes from get_orderby(request) and selected_columns from get_field_list, on both the RPC path (orderby around line 241) and top_events_timeseries (orderby around line 259). A request ordered by count() or -count() therefore ranks the top N groups by the sampled count while the returned series uses upsampled_count. Callers get the wrong groups, or the top-N query fails if it also references the rewritten alias. orderby and any count() in the top-N selected columns need the same transform as the timeseries columns.

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects always cache.get's before it knows the dataset is errors. That helper runs on every _get_event_stats call, including transaction, span, and metrics queries, and dashboard split runs it several times per request. options.get of the allowlist is already served from the in-process options cache; this adds a shared-cache RTT (and a hard dependency on that cache) on the events-stats hot path to avoid a cheaper lookup. A slow or failing cache delays or fails unrelated stats requests. The allowlist check should happen only after the dataset/query gate, and should not require a remote cache.

This change adds sentry-repo as a gitlink/submodule pointer to a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR base) with no .gitmodules entry and no relation to upsampling. Clones and CI that recurse into submodules, or tools that refuse gitlinks, will fail or nest a second checkout of this repo. The gitlink should be removed before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every newly denied resource reloads the full permission set

If the permission cache hits but checkPermission is false, Check always calls getIdentityPermissions, which ignores the cache and loads every scope for that user and action from the DB, then writes the cache back. Absence in a just-refreshed complete set is treated the same as a stale cache. Denial entries only dedupe the exact same name and folder, so a sequential sweep of unauthorized resources (list filtering, many GETs) issues one full permission query per resource per 30s instead of the previous single query per user+action. Concurrent checks share one singleflight, but sequential checks do not.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same cache-handling asymmetry: a cached permission denial triggers a fresh database lookup rather than being trusted. It emphasizes repeated queries instead of the golden comment's stale-grant security risk, but points to the same underlying Check logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed and does not cover deny-then-grant, renderer/anonymous key collision, or UID delimiter collisions.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same mismatch: the test comment claims cached permissions allow dash1, but the cache stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission does not grant access. The additional test-coverage concerns do not change this direct match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key joins name and folder with an underscore

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name, and parent with '_' and no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, and parent is often empty, so distinct resources share one key. For example name=foo, parent=bar and name=foo_bar, parent="" both become ..._foo_bar_, and name=abc, parent=de_f matches name=abc_de, parent=f. A deny for one resource then returns Allowed=false for the other for 30s with no permission or folder check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous denial cache keys caused by concatenating components with underscores without escaping, allowing collisions and incorrect cached permission denials. The candidate's first collision example is inaccurate, but it still clearly identifies the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins false denies and skips the DB re-query

Check returns Allowed=false as soon as permDenialCache has an entry for (namespace, subject id, action, name, parent), before reading permissions or the folder tree. That entry is written for every DB deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes it when permissions are granted or the folder cache is refreshed. A check that races ahead of the creator ACL insert (or any deny followed by a grant, including a new wildcard/admin role) therefore stays denied for the full TTL even though the new re-query path would now allow it. The same stickiness freezes inheritance failures caused by a stale folder tree: once denied, later requests never rebuild the tree or reload scopes. A slow in-flight query that snapshotted pre-grant rows can also Set the denial after a concurrent request already observed the grant, so retries keep failing for 30s. This recreates the 'creator cannot open what they just created' failure on the retry that the PR is meant to fix.

Denial cache key omits identity type and collides on id 0

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from checkReq.UserUID only, not the identity type or the canonical UID from GetUserIdentifiers. Anonymous checks use subject anonymous:0 and the renderer uses render:0 (both covered by tests), so both produce the same key for a given namespace, action, name, and folder. An anonymous deny of dashboards:read on a dashboard is then served to the renderer for 30s, and every anonymous retry refreshes that TTL, so image rendering/PDF of that dashboard can stay broken as long as anonymous checks keep missing. The reverse is also true for actions the renderer is denied. Numeric subjects (user:123) are likewise keyed separately from the resolved UID, so the same person does not share denial entries across id and uid forms, and a numeric id can collide with another identity whose id string matches.

After finding an ACTIVE Integration with no OrganizationIntegration, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. This pipeline never writes sender (build_integration only copies state["sender"], which nothing in the new flow sets), and older rows may not have that key or may store a non-dict. A missing or malformed sender raises KeyError/TypeError instead of the installation error page, so re-link/reinstall of those installations 500s and the security check never returns a controlled failure. The same block also re-fetches with status=ACTIVE and turns a non-active Integration into the generic authenticity error, which is a behavior change from the previous re-link path.

false_positives.candidate:
Token exchange drops the redirect_uri used to obtain the code

OAuthLoginView always sends redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect (built at the redirect just above), but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. OAuth 2.0 requires that if redirect_uri was included in the authorization request, the token request must repeat that exact value; GitHub otherwise rejects the code with bad_verification_code or redirect_uri_mismatch. TablesList still escape-doubles single quotes only and builds SELECT json_serialize_sql('<user SQL>'), then passes that string to RunCommands. The new enableSqlExpressions check in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery does not cover that path; the reader comment says it has not replaced the existing expression pipeline in transform.go. RunCommands and QueryFramesInto currently return "not implemented", so DuckDB is not invoked and this is not an active RCE. The CVE sink is still on the request path: quote-doubling does not make that statement safe, and any change that makes those methods succeed, or a caller that ignores the TablesList error and still executes, runs attacker-controlled SQL with no feature-flag gate. Reject in NewSQLCommand and Execute before formatting or dispatching SQL, and remove the json_serialize_sql interpolation.

Disabled SQL expressions are reported as unimplemented or invalid SQL

When SQL expressions are refused, ReadQuery returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is wrong: the feature existed and is being turned off for CVE-2024-9264, not left unimplemented. On the expression command path, NewSQLCommand still returns the public BadRequest "error reading SQL command" (sql-invalid-sql in pkg/expr/sql_command.go) for every SQL expression, because TablesList now always fails. Users and support will treat a security disable as a syntax error in their query. Return one stable message that SQL expressions are disabled.

No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected and not executed

This change is the CVE-2024-9264 fix (DuckDB removed, SQL expressions disabled) but it adds or updates no tests. Nothing asserts that a SQL expression fails closed on the production command path, that user SQL is not handed to an engine, or that turning on FlagSqlExpressions cannot restore execution. The mitigation is a stub whose methods return "not implemented"; restoring a real RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, or skipping the TablesList error and still calling Execute, would not fail CI. Add a test that builds a SQL expression through NewSQLCommand/Execute and expects a disable error without running the statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not re-check cache and can clobber a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock and later takes the write lock without reading entryPointAssetsCache again. Every caller that observed a nil cache (or is running in Dev) therefore reloads the manifest while holding the global mutex, then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. On a cold start, N concurrent calls all pass the nil check, queue on the write lock, and each performs a full file read; a later caller whose read fails stores nil and wipes the successful cache published by an earlier caller, so subsequent non-Dev requests miss and can return an error even though a valid asset set was already loaded. Re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock (and do not overwrite a non-nil cache with a failed load). The exclusive lock is also held across the manifest read, so those redundant loads are fully serialized.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: GetWebAssets fails to re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate it. The additional cache-clobbering discussion elaborates on the consequences of that same issue.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:

That copies the whole growing string on each ID. The new path is specifically for large batches (the test uses 32767, and the setting can be set higher), so one DELETE builds O(n^2) bytes of temporary strings — several seconds and heavy GC at 32k IDs, and much worse if the batch size is raised further. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful delete records the object name as the kind label

On a successful Storage.Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as the third argument. Every other call in this file passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, every distinct deleted name becomes a new series. That grows without bound for the process registry and any scraper, and the delete latency/error series can no longer be aggregated by kind.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: successful Delete passes the object name to recordStorageDuration instead of options.Kind, unlike other methods. The candidate adds potential metric-label consequences.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). When the apiserver handler returns, that parent context is cancelled, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never applies, and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection observe context.Canceled instead of finishing. Mode 3's legacy copy therefore does not land on the success path, so a rollback to legacy storage loses or stale-reads every write that was acknowledged from unified storage.

Per-object legacy writes are unordered

Each successful Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection fires an independent goroutine with no per-key queue, lock, or generation check. The handler returns as soon as unified storage succeeds, so a later delete (or newer update) can be applied to legacy before the earlier create/update. Legacy can then contain a resurrected object or an older spec while unified storage, which mode 3 reads, has the new state. Rollback or any legacy reader then serves data the API already deleted or overwrote. The closure also shares the request object with the caller; if Storage.Create returns that same pointer, the caller's continued use races with Legacy.Create.

Legacy update no longer persists the unified result

Update now passes the original objInfo into Legacy.Update after Storage.Update returns. The previous implementation computed the object once from unified storage and wrote that exact result to legacy through updateWrapper. In mode 3 the client resourceVersion comes from unified storage, so legacy GuaranteedUpdate's optimistic check fails with a conflict once the two backends' resource versions differ, and the safety copy is dropped. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, UpdatedObject runs against legacy's own old object and can persist a different spec. objInfo is also not guaranteed to be reusable after the first Update, so the async second call can fail or write a mutated object.

NotFound on unified delete skips legacy cleanup

Delete returns on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous mode 3 delete still removed the object from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. During migration, legacy can still hold objects that unified storage does not. Those deletes now fail to the client and leave the legacy row in place, so a fallback to legacy resurrects objects the API reported as gone.

Storage and legacy durations are recorded on the wrong series

When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration for a unified-storage failure, and Update does the same at line 129 with recordLegacyDuration. DeleteCollection's async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration, so the legacy outcome is counted as another storage observation and legacy delete-collection latency is never recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage failures to legacy and hide real legacy delete-collection failures.

Legacy write failures are not logged

The async Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, and Legacy.DeleteCollection calls only feed a boolean into the duration metric. The previous synchronous path logged the legacy error with the object identity. A timeout, conflict, or context cancellation now leaves unified storage and legacy diverged with no log line, so the safety copy can fail indefinitely without an operator-visible signal.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection do not track their goroutines. Shutdown can destroy legacy storage while a goroutine is still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which races with teardown and drops the safety copy for writes that were already acknowledged. There is no WaitGroup or drain anywhere in DualWriterMode3.

Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the legacy write

Success-path tests install legacy On expectations (Create around line 31, Update around line 313) but return as soon as the synchronous unified call finishes, and they never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. testify will not fail if the legacy call is skipped, and the goroutine can invoke the mock after the test has finished. Both stores also share one mock.Mock, so a single Create/Update expectation cannot prove which backend ran. The new cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (file mode 3 at line 132, unified mode 3 at line 191) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets the legacy playlist API after a k8s write. Those checks assume the legacy write is synchronous; with this mode 3 they race, and they fail outright if the request context cancels the legacy write.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key

The grafana branch of the filtered-rule map used to render GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}. The replacement GrafanaRuleListItem has no key, while the datasource and unknown branches still use key. As infinite scroll appends rows, React can reuse the wrong list-item instance, so action-menu and drawer state can attach to a different rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list views provide only a Prometheus rule, allowing the Silence notifications menu item to appear, but the drawer still requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Clicking the item therefore toggles state without rendering a drawer.

The list view now computes canPause and canDelete from Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the menu still renders Pause only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123) and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165). Those actions are gone from the new alert list; GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx locks this in by expecting exactly four menu items and never asserting Delete or Pause.

skipToken still grants Duplicate via Grafana create permission

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken) evaluates useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) instead of returning all-denied abilities. With no rule, loading is false, so MaybeSupported is AlwaysSupported and Duplicate is allowed whenever the user has Grafana AlertingRuleCreate. AlertRuleMenu ORs that result with the ruler result, so cloud and ruler-only rules show Duplicate for anyone who can create Grafana rules, even when the datasource ability denies it. Update and Delete do not leak because their allowed flag stays false, but Duplicate does.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and block update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (TODO on line 243). Every caller of useAlertRuleAbility, including the existing rules UI, will offer edit and delete on Mimir/enterprise federated groups. groupIdentifier does not carry source_tenants, so the check was dropped rather than moved.

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule detail back link returned to the current list, including filters. The new href is only /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view. Opening a rule from the list and using the in-app back control drops the user on the default alerting page instead of the filtered list.

Prometheus abilities treat only alerting rules as exportable

useAllRulerRuleAbilities allows ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently for any Grafana-managed rule (alerting or recording) via rulerRuleType.grafana.rule. useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates those same actions on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule. The list view relies on the Prometheus hook, so Grafana recording rules lose Export (and would also lose pause/restore/permanent delete once those menu items no longer require a ruler rule).

Creating and deleting rules are no longer distinguished

GrafanaGroupLoader used to match ruler and Prometheus rules and render ruler-only rules as Creating and Prometheus-only rules as Deleting (without edit or more actions). It now lists only Prometheus rules. Until Prometheus catches up, a just-created rule is missing from the group, and a just-deleted rule still appears as a normal rule with edit, silence, duplicate, and export. The tests that covered those states were removed rather than replaced.

isProvisionedPromRule reads provenance on a type that lacks it

isProvisionedPromRule takes PromRuleDTO and accesses promRule.provenance after prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule). That helper is not a type predicate, and PromRuleDTO (PromAlertingRuleDTO | PromRecordingRuleDTO) does not declare provenance — only GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase does. This is a TypeScript error, and RuleActionsButtons passes a Rule into this function, so provisioned detection for the clone flow may not typecheck. At runtime a non-Grafana rule short-circuits, but a Grafana rule is only treated as provisioned if the object happens to have provenance.

Early interpolation defeats the $__range split exclusion

runSplitQuery now runs every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper replaces Grafana range macros ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms) from request.scopedVars using the full request range. querySupportsSplitting then calls isQueryWithRangeVariable on the already-rewritten expr, so the $__range token is gone and the query is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these queries must not be split because the macro is meant to be interpolated on the backend against each request's own time range. After this change each chunk is executed with the full-range duration baked in (for example count_over_time({app="x"}[7d]) on every 1-day slice), so merged results overlap or over-count and Loki load grows with the selected range. The new tests only cover $__auto and $step, and the default test templateSrv does not expand $__range, so this production path is untested. Interpolate only after classifying queries on the raw expr, and leave $__range* in the expression sent to the backend.

Shard queries are template-interpolated twice, including ad-hoc filters

runShardSplitQuery now maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters), then splitQueriesByStreamShard rewrites those expressions with interpolateShardingSelector and calls runSplitQuery. runSplitQuery unconditionally applies applyTemplateVariables again on that rewritten expr, with the same request.filters still set. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: ad-hoc filters are inserted into the stream selector on each call, so a sharded query gets duplicate matchers (or a failed/misplaced insertion once `| drop __stream_shard__` is already in the LogQL). A second template replace can also expand `$` sequences that appeared in variable values. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (once here plus once per split group) and only uses an idempotent replace mock, so it locks in the double application instead of catching duplicate filters. Interpolate once, before shard selector injection, and do not run applyTemplateVariables again inside runSplitQuery for targets that are already interpolated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or unique cap. Concurrent anonymous logins that all observe count < deviceLimit all take the INSERT path and the table (and thus anonymous access) exceeds the configured limit. This is the common case when many new devices arrive together at the cap. The count and the insert/update need to be serialized (single transaction with a lock, or an insert that rechecks the cap) so the limit cannot be overrun.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend serializing the check and insert using a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached as success

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the 29-minute local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. On ErrDeviceLimitReached the first call correctly fails, but the cache entry is left in place and the next TagDevice for that same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache and returns nil. Authenticate treats nil as success, so anonymous access is granted and the device is never recorded. A client that retries once (or any later request within the TTL) bypasses the limit entirely. The cache is also not cleared on transient DB errors, so a failed write is treated as tagged and is not retried for 29 minutes. Set the cache only after a successful write, and do not treat a limit failure as a cache hit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is enforced only if the client sends a device id

The new auth denial depends on TagDevice, which returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing, and Authenticate then issues an anonymous identity. The header is optional and client-controlled, so omitting it never consumes a slot and never hits ErrDeviceLimitReached. A caller can also mint device_limit distinct ids to fill the quota (locking out honest frontends that do send the header) and then drop the header to keep its own anonymous access. As written, the limit cannot cap anonymous access. Enforcement needs a server-issued identifier, or requests without a tracked device must be denied once the cap is reached.

Provider signature change will not compile with existing wire code

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService no longer accepts anonstore.AnonStore and now requires db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. This package is constructed by the committed Wire injector (pkg/server/wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR and still calls the old signatures. The server build fails until wire is regenerated. Any other in-repo or enterprise caller that passed an AnonStore is also broken, and tests can no longer inject a fake store.

Device-limit failure is returned as an unclassified error

When the cap is hit, Authenticate returns the raw anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached sentinel (a plain fmt.Errorf). That is not an errutil or authn error, so the auth middleware treats it as an unexpected failure and typically responds with HTTP 500 rather than a controlled 401/403 and a user-facing device-limit message. It also shows up as a server error in logs. Return a typed unauthorized/forbidden auth error so the client chain and HTTP layer handle it as an access denial.

Limit tests miss the allow-existing path and auth enforcement

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only inserts a second, unknown device id against the store and expects ErrDeviceLimitReached. It never checks that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated once the cap is reached, and nothing covers TagDevice, the local cache, or Anonymous.Authenticate. Those are the paths that actually grant or deny access, so the cache-as-success bypass and the missing-header bypass are untested and would ship green.

device_limit is not added to default config

auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0), but conf/defaults.ini (and the docs generated from it) are not updated. Operators have no documented default, comment, or sample for the new cap, and 0-means-unlimited exists only in the store's if deviceLimit > 0 check. Add the key to the [auth.anonymous] section in defaults.ini with that meaning spelled out.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation path never loads fallback locale files

I18n.translate still only calls load_locale for config.locale, and the new ensure_loaded! helper is invoked only from ApplicationController#set_locale. The accelerator otherwise refuses to load YAML except for that one locale, while I18n::Backend::Fallbacks looks up SiteSetting.default_locale and :en in memory. Jobs, mailers, I18n.with_locale, and any I18n.t outside that before_filter therefore miss fallback strings (and plural rules) that exist on disk. Calls with no interpolation args then freeze the "translation missing" result in the LRU cache, so later loading the fallback locale does not repair that key until restart or eviction.

Cached translations ignore the fallback locale

The no-argument translation cache key is only the key, I18n.locale, and backend object id. FallbackLocaleList now resolves missing keys through SiteSetting.default_locale, which admins can change at runtime without I18n.reload!. A string that was filled from the old site locale stays cached under the user locale, so after a default-locale change users of incomplete locales keep seeing the previous language for hot keys until process restart or LRU eviction.

Fallbacks turned on in development and test

config.i18n.fallbacks = true was previously limited to production, profile, and the cloud66 production file, so development and test left missing keys visible. This initializer always includes I18n::Backend::Fallbacks and installs FallbackLocaleList, with no environment guard. In development and test, a key missing from the current locale now silently becomes the site-locale or English string instead of the missing-translation marker, which hides incomplete locale files and can change specs that set a non-English locale and assert on missing keys or exact untranslated output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Existing allow-list is deleted and never copied

The copy of `embeddable_hosts` is gated on `embeddable_hosts.cmd_tuples > 0` after a SELECT. PG::Result#cmd_tuples is 0 for SELECT (row count is `ntuples`). The INSERT loop never runs, then the migration deletes the `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` site settings. Any site that gets past the category lookup loses its allow-list and embedding starts rejecting every referer.

Import passes a category id through the name option

PostCreator is still called with `category:`, which previously received `SiteSetting.embed_category`, a category name (the migration joins that setting to `categories.name`). Nothing in this PR teaches PostCreator to treat that option as an id, so embedded topic creation will either raise or land in the uncategorized category instead of the host's chosen category.
